4d5e1f5c1fab6083: Artificial intelligence has become part of the zeitgeist. And while it’s a polarizing topic, Linda Rabieh has a unique take on AI: “It’s good for business. Our business, of humanistic thinking.” As senior lecturer in the Concourse program, one of MIT’s first-year learning communities, Rabieh has been introducing students to the “business” since 2010.  “What AI has been useful for is making very vivid to students today the question of what it means to be human,” she adds. “They’re meeting this question with a new urgency. What is intelligence? Is it only mathematical intelligence? Is it only an aggregation of information? Or is human intelligence something different?” AI is just one of countless thorny topics that bubble up in Concourse, which offers first-year MIT students a foundation in the humanities, alongside math and science General Institute Requirement courses taught by Concourse faculty. Studying “great books” and literary luminaries — Plato, Homer, Aristotle, Wordsworth and Coleridge, to name a few — provides a springboard for rich conversations and spirited debates. A “mini-liberal arts college within MIT” Concourse was founded in 1970 to enable humanities, engineering, and science faculty to collaborate on curriculum, cultivating a “concourse” of ideas. Now it’s a place, Rabieh says, “where students who come primarily to MIT for world-class science, math, and engineering can also have a traditional liberal education, exploring fundamental questions of human existence, reading the great books, engaging in intense, vigorous debate about these questions.” “I often describe Concourse as a mini-liberal arts college within MIT,” says Assistant Director Sasha Rickard ’19, an alumna of the program. “A lot of students tell us that Concourse is a big part of the reason they decided on MIT instead of [other schools].” Concourse accepts 50 first-year students each year. Johnnie Jones VI, a senior in mathematics and Concourse teaching assistant (TA) and debate fellow, marvels at the diversity of students the program attracts — “athletes, people who are interested in humanities, people who have no experience in humanities,” he says. “Somehow, 50 people every year self-select into this space, and magic happens.” Connection and “cross-pollination” Part of that magic is the sense of community that Concourse fosters. The program has a dedicated space in Building 16 with a classroom, seminar room, lounge, and kitchen. Students receive advising and participate in community events throughout the year. Since they overlap in their humanities, math, and science classes, as well as outside the classroom, they get to know each other and their instructors well. “There’s a lot of cross-pollination of conversation and ideas,” Rabieh says.  During the weekly Friday advising seminar, students gather over lunch to discuss assigned texts or hold debates. In the fall, topics focus broadly on the human condition, and in the spring, students consider practical political or moral issues such as gene therapy, immigration, and gun control. Several debates are held in conjunction with the MIT Civil Discourse Project, which has collaborated with Concourse since 2023. Many students stay involved in the program after their first year. Some serve as TAs, debate fellows, or associate advisors.  “There’s very much a sense of wanting to be guides and supports and set an example for the incoming students,” Rickard says. Upper-level students also take Concourse electives, hang out in the lounge, and participate in community events. Learning to think things through Taking multiple classes together, sharing meals, and spending time together outside the classroom — these common experiences build a level of trust that allows students to hold deep conversations. The result is a transformative experience. Rickard has noticed that incoming first-years tend to fall into two categories: those who think they already know the answers to political or philosophical questions, and those who have no opinion because they think there’s no definitive answer. Over time, she explains, “some students come to understand that they need to learn from others, and others learn that they really can think for themselves, and they do have something to say.” “Students learn the importance of judgment in non-quantitative areas,” Rabieh says. MIT students excel at quantitative reasoning, she adds, but “you can’t just show which political policy is right and which is wrong … and one reason I think MIT students shy away from those kinds of issues is because they don’t see a way to think through them. Concourse teaches them a way to think about moral and political questions in a rigorous way that isn’t quantitative.” That rings true for Jones. “Overwhelmingly, the greatest skill Concourse has given me, more than just teaching me things, is teaching me how to work through ideas myself — really making possible the ability to, even after a long day of work, sit down with a great book and have a conversation with someone who was alive 300 years ago about things that matter to me,” he says. Stewarding the “ethos of Concourse” into its next chapter As Concourse continues into its next half-century, a new leader has taken the helm. Ford Professor of Political Science Lily Tsai was recently named director after Anne McCants, the Ann F. Friedlaender Professor of History, stepped down. Colleagues laud McCants for 14 years of steady leadership; cultivating a robust, collaborative advising program; advocating for a whole-student approach; and for her passion for teaching. McCants says she relished interacting with Concourse students in a sustained way — often for all four years — and learning not only from them, but also colleagues. “Having a group of committed educators from different disciplines in sustained conversation is a remarkable feature of Concourse. In our normal faculty roles, we are siloed off from those whose fields of study are not ours. I will miss those interactions as much as I do the ones with the students.” Tsai assumes the role as the Institute expands efforts to broaden connections between the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) and other fields. Those efforts include the Compass Initiative, which Tsai co-leads with other faculty from across SHASS; the MIT Human Insight Collaborative; and the creation of shared faculty positions within the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. “The ethos of Concourse is thrilling to me,” Tsai says. “Through reflection and debate about what we value individually and collectively, Concourse students cultivate the skills and habits of mind that prepare them to be not only excellent engineers and scientists, but also responsible citizens and leaders. At a time when the whole world is seeking to ground our use of powerful technologies in thoughtful, principled judgment, Concourse seems all the more vital, and I’m eager to champion the teaching and learning that the program does so well.”

8588cf61af9ff366: A phishing campaign targeting advertising managers by impersonating Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus to steal credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes has added a fake Muse Ads product to its lure lineup – just eight days after Meta launched its personal AI agent. Meta announced Muse on September 8, and by September 17, a very convincing website – museads.ai – for a product called Muse Ads that promised to help advertisers reach buyers and run sponsored placements popped up online. “The operators already had the platform, so adapting it to a new brand can take minutes,” Oleg Zaytsev, lead security researcher at Island, told The Register. “The striking part is how quickly they turned a timely announcement into a credible reason for someone to act. The same platform could then be repackaged around other familiar tasks, from connecting a business tool to claiming a refund or applying for a job.” The security startup spotted the Muse Ads webpage, and upon digging into the scam uncovered that just the page was new. “Its code, from the sign-in forms to the fake browser window, came from a wider operation that had already run fake ad products for Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Manus,” Zaytsev and fellow Island researcher Ofek Ronen wrote in a blog post published Tuesday. All of these products served as lures for browser-in-the-browner (BitB) attacks designed to trick agency staff, media buyers, and manager-account administrators into handing over their advertising account credentials – along with stored payment methods and client accounts – to digital thieves. “For victims, the potential cost is loss of access to an advertising account, unauthorized ad spend, and exposure of linked client accounts,” Zaytsev told The Register. How the scam works BitB is a clever phishing technique originally detailed by a researcher called mr.d0x in 2022. It involves building a fake login window directly inside a legitimate one. The fake window looks like the real thing, featuring an address bar, title, and URL, but it's just an overlay to steal users’ credentials. According to Zaytsev, this one has likely proved very lucrative for its criminal operators, with hundreds of victim submissions to the platform, and activity still ongoing. “From one frontend alone, we observed submissions involving roughly 200 distinct email addresses over about a month,” he told us. “The operators used the same platform across many similar sites, so we estimate the campaign-wide volume is substantially higher.” Each phony ad product has its own page, with ChatGPT promising users a Monday Google Ads brief, Gemini offering manager account and linked-client support, Claude an advertising portal, Perplexity pitching campaign planning and spend audits, and Manus providing a private Meta integration. Each fake product page also has a “connect” button. When the victim clicks “connect,” it opens the browser-in-browser overlay, with a fake address bar showing accounts.google.com, or an Okta tenant to gain the victim’s trust. The real browser, however, stays on the phishing domain and steals credentials when the victim types them in. A human operator running the campaign sees each submission and chooses what the victim sees and is prompted to do. This includes asking for another password, requesting an SMS or Okta authenticator code to bypass MFA, showing a Google approval code or Okta push request, or displaying a QR code. The platform supports Google, Meta, TikTok, and Okta workflows, and the browser overlay adapts to whatever the victim runs: Window, macOS, iOS, ot Android, and even mimics Safari’s URL pill, Chrome’s custom tabs, and a dark mode. And while the researchers told us they haven’t identified the people operating the kit or found a name under which it’s sold, the operators did expose older source code through misconfigured public GitHub repositories that connected this to a campaign to a larger operation. In addition to the AI ad pages, this operation also used fake refund claims and job recruitment sites as lures with separate builds for Adidas, Google Careers, Robert Half, Tesla, and Louis Vuitton. All of these pages run on one Next.js and Socket.IO stack. Many of the pages also used Vercel frontends with Railway or Render services behind them for state and commands. “A new brand or polished page doesn’t necessarily mean a new attack. Operators can change the lure quickly, but the workflow still has to move someone onto a site they control, collect credentials, and steer them through authentication,” Zaytsev said. “Security teams should maintain a continuous baseline of trusted domains, check the real browser address, and connect similar behavior across different sites,” he added. “Attackers can generate a convincing website quickly; building the domain history and reputation of a legitimate service is much harder. AI can help defenders keep pace with AI-generated websites, especially as they become more convincing and appear more quickly.”. ®

8373a76c0750b53d: Life is remarkably selective. Life relies on many molecules with what is termed "handedness"—they're chemically identical but are mirror images of each other. Most chemical reactions will make a 50-50 mix of the left- and right-handed forms of a chemical, but life uses only one of them. In fact, because of the differences between left- and right-handed chemicals, most of the key enzymes used by organisms will fail to work if they're presented with chemicals that have the wrong handedness.

That poses a bit of a challenge for origin-of-life research, as we're forced to explain how a world that may have started with an even mix of left- and right-handed chemicals produced organisms that only used one of them.

Today's Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to two individuals, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who discovered chemical reactions could be biased, producing large excesses of one of the two forms of a chemical.

4f1b1687445cacba: AWS has offered multiple open-source strategies for holding AI agents accountable, and now it’s adding a full-on sandbox to this stack. Dubbed Strands Box, the new solution uses OS-level isolation and some of AWS’ other recent open-source AI control tools to, ostensibly, retain greater control over autonomous AI agents’ behavior. “Agents increasingly run in ‘YOLO mode,’ approving every action without human review,” the AWS team explained in its announcement. “The usual solution to this problem is a sandbox … but access is only part of what we want to control.” The problem with containers and microVMs typically used to isolate AI agents, as AWS explains it, is that their strong isolation doesn’t come with contextual rule enforcement. In other words, when a containerized or virtualized agent gets hold of a tool, there may be no stopping it from doing whatever it wants - like deleting a production database, or gaining access to the internet and doing dog knows what. That’s where the other open-source tools inside Strands Box come in: It uses the Dogwood Local Engine to give the policy engine in Box temporal awareness, so tool calls can be checked against not only what the agent wants to do, but what it’s already done. As one example, AWS noted that an agent could be allowed to post status updates to Slack, but no more than three times every ten minutes to prevent it from spamming its human operators. An AWS spokesperson further explained that Box could be used to control when an agent can perform a Git push, or it could be used to put a cap on API calls that could end up costing a small fortune. Additionally, Strands Box includes Strands Shell and Monty for Python, which expose shell and Python operations to the same Dogwood policy engine and event history, making agentic actions clearer to developers and allowing policies to account for what an agent is trying to do. AWS VP and distinguished engineer Marc Brooker, one of the folks behind Dogwood and Strands Box, explained to The Register that the interpreters are a key part of making agentic behavior more intelligible, which allows for devs to write more precise policies to prevent agents from taking bad actions. “Box’s Shell and Python interpreters expose operations such as file deletions, while its gateways expose API requests and tool calls,” Brooker told us in an email. “Policies can then account for the action being attempted and earlier activity.” Box, Brooker added, enforces those rules without trusting or relying on agents to actually follow instructions, which should ideally prevent them from running roughshod over their operators’ wishes. As for the reason behind AWS’ push to develop open-source tools like Dogwood, the Dogwood Local Engine, and Strands Box, Brooker said that AWS wants to find the right balance between boundaries and policies that prevent agentic AI disasters of the kind we regularly report. “Box enforces the policies developers configure, deterministically, and the agent can't talk its way around these rules,” Brooker explained, though he added that, even with properly configured permissions, an agentic action can still produce an unwanted result. “Developers remain responsible for deciding what access to grant and where human review is needed,” Brooker added - in other words, don’t let your YOLO mode go too YOLO. A bit of human oversight is still necessary. “Agent safety is an area where the industry still has significant work to do, and we're committed to continuing to invest in it, both inside the AWS cloud and in open source,” Brooker said. Strands Box supports any agent or harness one wants to confine within its walls and is available on GitHub now, though only for macOS for the time being. Linux support is in development, and AWS told us a Windows client is “on our radar,” but neither has a planned release date. Deployment to platforms like AgentCore, ECS, and Kubernetes is also planned. ®

01f3e88e940a3f3c: The attorneys general of Florida, Iowa, Montana, and Nebraska have sued ubiquitous networking and smart home tech maker TP-Link, alleging its security claims were misleading and it hadn't properly disclosed ties to China. The company has a large presence in US retail and the tech channel, especially in consumer routers, with stats from Circana asserting it had around 36.6 percent US market share by units and 31 percent by dollars in 2024. The complaint [PDF] accuses California-based TP-Link Systems, whose brand originated in Shenzhen, of deceptive and unfair marketing practices concerning its routers' security and its connections to China. It cites exploitation of TP-Link devices by Chinese and Russian state-backed hackers. The suit also claims TP-Link allegedly concealed facts about its "past and ongoing ties to the People's Republic of China," accuses it of having a supply chain that's reliant on PRC players, repeated firmware vulnerabilities, and being subject to Chinese laws that force companies to cooperate with state intelligence. According to the states' attorneys general, the hardware vendor still relies on Chinese companies for research and development and manufacturing operations, despite previously claiming to have moved into Vietnam after severing ties with China. The complaint alleges that only 0.5 percent of components used at TP-Link's Vietnamese plant, measured by value, are bought in Vietnam, with "all other inputs" imported "from or through China." The complaint also claims that a US-designated Chinese military company carried out construction work at the Vietnamese factory, challenging TP-Link's assurances about its supply chain's security. The complaint cites 2025 testimony [PDF] from former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce that TP-Link's share of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and small-office/home-office (SoHo) routers at at least 60 percent. Lawyers pointed to various snippets from TP-Link's marketing materials. These included claims that its HomeShield product "covers all security scenarios" and, on a version of its website available in November 2025, provides a "100 percent safeguard" for network security. The complaint argues that TP-Link's security assurances were misleading because its routers contained critical vulnerabilities. It further cites Joyce's that TP-Link routers were among the brands exploited in the China-linked Volt Typhoon and Flax Typhoon campaigns. The complaint also alleges that TP-Link's privacy policies permit it to collect customer data and share it with affiliates without disclosing how its Chinese connections and China's intelligence laws could expose that information to Chinese intelligence agencies. "Iowans' sensitive data and our national security is at risk because of TP-Link and their connection to the communist Chinese government," said Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird. "TP-Link tells Iowans its routers are safe, our personal data is secure, and that they have no ties to China. They are not telling the truth. It's time to hold China and China-backed companies accountable." "TP-Link's false statements and deceptive advertising are a violation of Montana law," said Attorney General Austin Knudsen. "As a result of their nefarious practices, millions of Americans have unknowingly invited a foreign adversary into their living rooms and put their personal information at risk. "I will do everything I can as Attorney General to hold TP-Link accountable and protect our privacy and security." Steve Kovsky, corporate affairs officer for TP-Link Systems Inc., said the lawsuits were based on false premises, did nothing to advance national security, and unfairly penalized a US company. Kovsky added that the company has spent months providing officials with clear documentation showing that it is not owned or controlled by any foreign government and that its devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam. "Any claims that our products present a threat to user security or grant unauthorized network access to foreign governments are baseless," he said. "TP-Link Systems is a US company that complies with US privacy and data protection laws. We perform comprehensive security testing and rely on trusted third-party security labs for additional scrutiny to ensure our products meet the highest security standards and are recognized as among the most secure on the market. "We meet or exceed all industry best practices for monitoring and preventing vulnerabilities and actively support our customers to mitigate any issues that occur as they are identified. We do not, and will not, share customer network data with foreign governments or unauthorized third parties. "We stand fully behind the security of our products, the integrity of our company and our people, and our commitment to serving the best interests of our customers in the United States and globally. We look forward to refuting these baseless allegations in court." The allegations echo those made by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose office sued TP-Link earlier this year over its Chinese connections and router security. US officials began weighing restrictions on TP-Link router sales in 2024. In March 2026, the FCC imposed broader restrictions [PDF] on new foreign-produced router models, barring new equipment authorizations unless an exemption is granted. Previously authorized models were not automatically banned. ®

8c53a494f4c7a130: MOSCOW: Russia's health regulator said on Wednesday there were no risks of an epidemic breaking out in Siberia after a plague institute worker there died, as the World Health Organization pressed Moscow for more information about her cause of death.

Russian authorities say the 28-year-old laboratory worker died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump. Around 200 people were initially placed in quarantine.

Global health officials - as well as the world's media - have been particularly alert to pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the Covid-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China.

However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined. The WHO estimates the risk of the Russia incident to the general public to be low based on currently available information.

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's health watchdog, said in a statement on Wednesday it was winding down precautionary measures it had put in place after concluding there was no risk of an epidemic and that it had shared its latest information with the WHO.

No cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with the deceased worker, Darya Shipilova, it said, and 90 per cent of those placed in quarantine had been released after nearly 5,000 lab tests had failed to detect any dangerous pathogens.

It said Shipilova had been vaccinated and had therefore been "immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked." It did not say though what had caused the pneumonia which killed her or how she fell ill.
WHO CALLS FOR MORE INFORMATION
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the WHO in Geneva, said earlier on Wednesday that his organisation needed more information from Russia to understand what had happened.

"WHO has requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause," he said on X.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."
KREMLIN CRITICISES 'FALSE INFORMATION' IN MEDIA
The Kremlin said Russia had properly informed the WHO about the incident in line with established procedures.

When asked about the WHO's request to respond to reports about a second person in Siberia allegedly falling ill, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged caution when it came to using media reports as a reference for what was happening.
"There is a great deal of media coverage, and the vast majority of what the media are reporting about this situation is false information," said Peskov.
He advised the media and others to rely on information provided by the health regulator. It did not immediately respond to a Reuters comment request on Wednesday about the WHO's questions.
EXACT CAUSE OF DEATH REMAINS UNKNOWN
Some Western media outlets have reported — citing unnamed "Russian media" — that a second person in Siberia had died, saying they had died of plague.

Reuters was unable to find any such stories in Russian media or any evidence that a second person in Siberia had died although some bloggers on social media were making — without evidence — such assertions.
Contacted by Reuters, the WHO said it had nothing further to add on the matter beyond what Tedros — who was due to give a press conference later on Wednesday — had already posted on X.
Tedros' call for more information echoed that of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has also said Moscow needs to share more information about the incident.
Pneumonia, a lung infection, can have a variety of causes including plague as well as other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as flu or Covid-19.--REUTERS

200daad9bdf8608b: SpaceX has acknowledged the need for satellite operators to collaborate to avoid collisions and has taken the unusual step of sharing imagery showing how close spacecraft are coming to each other. The company has called on other operators to share their satellites' ephemeris (a set of parameters describing the position and velocity of a spacecraft over time) to facilitate timely avoidance maneuvers. "In 2026," the company wrote, "Starlink encountered conjunctions with about 650 unique maneuvering third-party satellites, with only about half of them actually sharing ephemeris. "Some operators don't share ephemeris out of a concern that sharing upcoming maneuvers gives away proprietary information. In other circumstances, operators are willing to share data, but are unable to receive permission from the government to do so. "Such policies are counterproductive, and largely only serve to create preventable collision risk between satellites." "Over six months," the company went on, "Starlink observed ~164,000 conjunctions where time of closest approach (TCA) was within four hours after an unannounced manoeuvre. "While not all of these conjunctions were high-risk, they represent cases where Starlink would not have sufficient information to reliably avoid the other vehicle if the other operator’s action created a high-risk conjunction. "In many cases, the lack of high-accuracy post-manoeuvre trajectory information can cause such conjunctions to go unnoticed, giving operators a false sense of confidence and not realising how much risk their actions are creating." How many sats is that again? It's all worthy stuff, until you consider that SpaceX has applied for permission to operate 100,000 Starlink satellites and up to 1 million Starmind AI satellites. Arguably that is a substantial contribution to orbital overcrowding. Not to worry though – space isn't really getting crowded, according to SpaceX. "A good analogy is air travel," the company wrote. "Airspace around the world has grown more congested since aviation began. Yet air travel is the safest form of transport on Earth in part because every aircraft publishes a flight plan and then continuously broadcasts its position during flight." Er, kind of. Although if aircraft collide, the debris falls rapidly to Earth, rather than lingering in the sky and potentially striking more aircraft weeks or months later. Plus, SpaceX is helpfully not counting other debris, from spent rocket casings to flakes of paint, that also pose a hazard in orbit. The company noted its successes, where Starlink satellites successfully dodged other vehicles. One in October 2025 occurred when the other satellite made an unexpected maneuver, reducing the predicted miss distance from 9 km to a bottom-clenching 57 meters. Another example happened in August 2026, when the risk was identified too late for the Starlink satellite to move out of the way, and the satellite had to "duck" instead, slewing to present a narrower profile. "The vehicles ultimately passed within 134 metres of each other," the company said. "This approach could have been prevented if the other object shared its manoeuvre ahead of time." SpaceX was keen for operators to connect to sites such as space-safety.com and talked up its Stargaze service, which uses star trackers on the Starlink fleet to observe nearby objects in orbit. A far cry from 2019, when a Starlink satellite failed to move out of the way of the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Aeolus Earth-observation satellite due to a bug in SpaceX's on-call paging system. There is no shortage of companies with capabilities to monitor and advise on traffic in orbit. Neuraspace, for example, springs to mind. As the company's CEO Chiara Manfletti observed, humanity has not done a particularly good job of looking after the space above the planet. While the technology used to prevent satellite collisions is impressive, and data sharing should be encouraged, we can't help but wonder whether another solution might be to not launch tens of thousands more satellites into orbit in the first place. Manfletti told The Register that the problem was very real. She said, "As the number of satellites increases, knowing where an object is today is no longer sufficient. Manoeuvrability is becoming essential, and operators increasingly need timely, accurate information about where other spacecraft intend to be, including planned manoeuvres." "Initiatives such as SpaceX's space-safety platform are certainly welcome. But the long-term solution cannot depend on every operator joining a single company's system. What we ultimately need is a federated and interoperable space-traffic ecosystem in which operators can securely exchange trusted trajectory and intent information across different platforms, organisations and national systems. "Neuraspace has reached out to SpaceX to enable such coordination on behalf of our customers. We have extended an open hand, and it would be a strong sign of leadership for SpaceX to take it — demonstrating that improving safety in orbit ultimately requires cooperation not only within individual platforms, but across them." ®

b909f726566177be: GAZA CITY: Israel carried out new strikes in Gaza on Wednesday as it marked the third anniversary of the Oct 7 attacks by Hamas, with Palestinian officials reporting three people dead.
Loud bangs across the border in Gaza were audible from the site of the Nova music festival just as family members gathered at dawn to mourn the more than 300 revellers killed three years earlier.
In Gaza City, Al-Shifa hospital reported two people killed in an Israeli strike overnight.
Gaza's civil defence identified one of the dead as Mohamed Tamous and said he was a volunteer for the agency, which serves as an emergency rescue service under Hamas.

The Israeli military said it struck and killed "two Hamas fighters who had exited Kamal Adwan Hospital in the northern Gaza Strip," adding that one had "planted explosives... in the area of the Yellow Line with the intention of harming IDF troops."
The so-called Yellow Line demarcates the areas under Hamas and Israeli military control in the Gaza Strip.
The military identified one of those killed in the strike as Tamous, whom it said was a sniper in Hamas's military wing while simultaneously working for the civil defence.
In the southern city of Khan Yunis, Nasser Hospital said that a 60-year-old man, Hisham Ibrahim Abu Mustafa, was killed in an Israeli strike and that others were injured.

On the third anniversary of the first day of the war in Gaza, living conditions remain dire in the coastal Palestinian territory, despite a US-brokered ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025.
"After three years of siege, killing and destruction, Israel has turned the Gaza Strip into an uninhabitable place," said Gaza City resident Mahmoud Abu Hasira.
Hundreds of thousands of displaced people still live in tent cities and makeshift shelters that sprawl on beaches or next to piles of rubble from bombed-out residential buildings.

"We once had homes, but now we have lost our loved ones, whose bodies still lie beneath the rubble," said Bassam Nasser, a resident of Beit Hanoun, a now largely destroyed city in Gaza's north, who was displaced in the early days of the war.
Israel says it controls about 60 per cent of Gaza, on the territory's outer perimeter including Beit Hanoun, while most of the Palestinian population lives in the remaining Hamas-controlled areas.
Though Israel eased its restrictions on aid trucks entering Gaza after the ceasefire, Ahmed Nasser, another resident of Gaza City, told AFP that life remained desperately hard.
"The war and the famine have left us hungry, fearful and displaced, living in tents and struggling with soaring prices," he said.

Israel's military offensive has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Since the ceasefire was declared last October, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,460 people in Gaza, according to the ministry.--AFP

"The crew was informed that the passenger intended to collect luggage containing vape products for the onward flight (to Manila) and that the passenger would personally handle the customs clearance process.

CGT Asia said the flight's operating crew were not involved in the customs clearance process in Laos.

After being informed about the number of luggage involved, it said the crew raised operational and safety concerns, including the unusually large quantity of baggage and the possible presence of lithium batteries or potentially dangerous goods.
"Prior to receiving information from the Lao authorities, neither CGT Asia nor the operating flight crew had knowledge that the luggage allegedly contained illicit drugs or controlled substances.

"The operating crew had already refused carriage of the baggage before becoming aware of its alleged contents. The luggage was not accepted for carriage and was not loaded onto the aircraft at Luang Prabang International Airport.

"Subsequently, the relevant Lao authorities inspected and took control of the luggage and advised that the baggage was suspected of containing a significant quantity of illicit drugs or controlled substances concealed within or among the declared items," it said.

This includes a pilot who owns the company that operated the private charter flight at the centre of the drug trafficking case.
f5f12c88b812e317: PETALING JAYA: Bersama membentangkan belanjawan negara bayangan, yang memperkenalkan semula cukai barang dan perkhidmatan (GST) tetapi pada kadar 5% serta menggantikan beberapa skim bantuan tunai dengan bantuan bulanan bersasaran.
Parti itu berkata mengehadkan GST pada kadar 5% selama 10 tahun akan datang akan memberikan kepastian kepada isi rumah dan perniagaan, selain mengekang kesan GST ke atas inflasi pada masa depan.
"Berdasarkan anggaran Bersama, GST pada kadar 5% boleh menjana sekitar RM76.1 bilion, atau 3.3% daripada KDNK, berbanding RM59.4 bilion yang dijangka dikutip melalui SST pada tahun 2026.
"Ini menghasilkan tambahan hasil sekitar RM16.7 bilion," katanya dalam dokumen belanjawan bayangan.
Bersama turut mencadangkan skim Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) dan Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) digantikan dengan pemberian RM200 sebulan kepada 60% isi rumah terbawah (B60).

Ia turut mencadangkan supaya setiap kanak-kanak warganegara Malaysia berumur bawah 18 tahun menerima RM50 sebulan, terhad kepada lima orang anak bagi setiap isi rumah, bersamaan manfaat maksimum RM250 sebulan atau RM3,000 setahun bagi setiap isi rumah.
Bersama turut berkata kerajaan sewajarnya mengkaji cadangan dan kerangka perundangan, teknologi dan pentadbiran bagi Cukai Pembayaran Elektronik Runcit (REPT) antara 2027 hingga 2029.
"Tiada REPT akan dikenakan sepanjang tempoh pembangunan ini. Tertakluk kepada kebolehlaksanaan kerangka tersebut, REPT boleh mula dilaksanakan pada tahun 2030 pada kadar 0.5%," katanya.
"REPT pada kadar 0.5% ke atas asas ini berpotensi menjana sekitar RM9.1 bilion setahun, sebelum mengambil kira pengecualian dan perubahan tingkah laku."
Katanya, langkah-langkah berkenaan, antara lain, boleh membantu Malaysia menurunkan defisit fiskal dan mencapai lebihan belanjawan menjelang 2035 -- buat kali pertama sejak 1997.
258958e274f2510a: A suspected Italian attacker armed with a malware-controlling poem has infected more than 3,000 servers since April, breaking into enterprise AI infrastructure to mine cryptocurrency and add compromised systems to its growing botnet. This is the first case of “adversarial poetry” - an AI jailbreak technique that turns harmful prompts into poems to trick LLMs into bypassing safety guardrails - that Lumen’s Black Lotus Labs, which has been tracking the PoeLLM malware, has seen in real-world attacks. “This is a first for us,” the researchers told The Register via email. “While we can't get inside the threat actor's head, we think the attacker might have used a poem because it serves as a perfect vehicle for hiding an important message,” they added. “To anyone who comes across it, this is simply a poem on GitHub. It has no links, no files to download, no encrypted text that could easily be flagged as malicious, even by advanced models. There would be no reason for any security researcher to identify this poem as malicious - or know about the IP address hidden within it - unless they had access to the malware referencing it.” PoeLLM malware has been active since at least April, impacting more than 3,000 servers primarily located in the US and Western Europe, and it continues to infect new victims. At its peak, the malware infected more than 800 active servers per day. The malware abuses - and scans for - open source AI systems and services. Most of the victims were running vulnerable, internet-facing versions of LiteLLM and Ollama. Additionally, hundreds of victims were running Gotenberg, a PDF converter, and software development platform Gitea. In addition to these open source tools, the attacker may have targeted commercial software including Ivanti Sentry. The threat hunters first spotted the PoeLLM malware while investigating an Ivanti Sentry vulnerability, CVE-2026-10520. “In early June 2026, a compromised Ivanti Sentry victim contacted a dedicated server at 5.78.73[.]122,” according to a Wednesday report shared with The Register. “Shortly after contacting this C2, the Ivanti Sentry victim began scanning for other vulnerable devices.” How adversarial poetry works Black Lotus Labs attributed the PoeLLM malware to an Italian-speaking criminal, and named the financially motivated campaign Canto Incognito because it hides the malicious commands in a poem posted to a GitHub repository. “Comments within the malware and on the attacker’s GitHub pages are in Italian, and netflow analyzed by Black Lotus Labs suggests that the attacker is located in Italy,” the threat-hunters told us, adding that they believe the campaign targets AI systems and that the poem itself was written by AI. The malware deploys XMRig and Iron miners, and connects victims to Kryptex mining infrastructure. In addition to using compromised GPU hardware powering AI workloads to mine cryptocurrency, PoeLLM also turns victims' machines into vulnerability scanners and exploit servers, which allows the attacker to compromise even more vulnerable systems. The researchers’ investigation indicates that the cryptojacking miscreant - aka GitHub user “ejejejdfbbebe” - made the first GitHub commit with the adversarial poem on April 13. The repo is a fork of the nodejs.org website source code, and the file is called “dash.css.” Inside the file, there’s a poem titled “On the Nature of Connection,” which has been updated 11 times since its initial commit. Here’s the most current version, as of September: In the silent hum of driver, the machines begin to speak, Each pulse of diode threading light through copper veins. we taught the dark to carry meaning, byte by byte — A language built from lightning, cold and clean. Beyond the wall of encryption, a signal finds its way, the tick of distant servers answering back. Data moves like water through the cracks of ordered thought, and somewhere in the code, the world stays on track. Here’s the adversarial piece: the malware finds its current command-and-control (C2) server from keywords in the poem, and when the operator changes the poem, the infected systems find the new C2 location. It does this by parsing the poem, extracting certain words and phrases, and then converting them to numbers using a hard-coded dictionary in the body of the malware. Black Lotus Labs says the logic for C2 discovery works like this: The function “extract_poem_phrase_field” extracts three words/phrases from the body of the poem, case-insensitively: Word 1: text between "In the silent hum of " and "," Word 2: text between "each pulse of " and " threading" Word 3: text between "Beyond the wall of " and "," 0x44a8db–0x44a99b extracts the fourth word differently: Find " of distant servers" Walk backward to the previous whitespace Require the 4 bytes before the word to be "the " Use the word after "the " as Word 4 The four words are then matched to corresponding numbers, which combine to form the IPv4 address hosting the server. Here’s what the C2 conversion looks like with the key: Black Lotus Labs’ write-up lists all the C2 IP addresses, plus when they were first and last seen, so be sure to check that out. More AI infrastructure = larger attack surface As enterprises increasingly use AI in their operations, they also expand their attack surface. And, as we have repeatedly seen, security remains an afterthought in AI deployments. “The Canto Incognito campaign appears to be relatively unique in its targeting of multiple AI-related services,” the researchers told The Register. “Other notable campaigns this year, including the LiteLLM supply chain compromise, focused on a single service and impacted roughly 2,500 victims, according to open sources. The collection of more than 3,000 PoeLLM victims appears to exhibit multiple vulnerable services at any given time.” For comparison: The LiteLLM supply chain attack, which began with a compromised Trivy build, potentially exposed more than 2,500 companies and 434,000 CI/CD pipelines worldwide, according to CloudSEK security researchers. The PoeLLM malware developer “has been extremely successful in identifying vulnerable servers, deploying exploits, and conscripting victims to continue expanding the campaign,” Black Lotus Labs said. “If the actor had only focused on one or two vulnerabilities, the potential victim pool might have quickly dried up, but the expanding scope allowed for a bigger, more powerful (and more profitable) botnet.” They told us they expect to see more of these types of attacks in the near future. “AI makes it easier to deploy tools like LiteLLM, Ollama, or Gotenberg, but AI isn't always checking to make sure those services are patched and protected from attackers,” the researchers said. “As more AI-enabled servers come online, malware like PoeLLM will continue to spread.”®
209600d881595413: KUALA LUMPUR: A 27-year-old SUV driver was detained today after he allegedly refused to stop following a police convoy escorting Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi.
City Traffic Investigation and Enforcement Department chief Assistant Commissioner Mohd Zamzuri Mohd Isa said the incident occurred at 9.20am on the Shah Alam Expressway (KESAS) towards Klang.
"The Honda CR-V, driven by a 27-year-old local man, was following the police convoy escorting the deputy prime minister from Kajang to Sunway Medical Centre in Subang Jaya.
"A police escort in the convoy warned the SUV driver not to follow the convoy.
"However, the man refused to comply and continued following the convoy. His actions were feared to have endangered the safety of the convoy and other road users," he said in a statement.
Following that, he said the man was detained by the enforcement division for further action.
He said the incident did not involve any collision, accident or other untoward incident.
Zamzuri said police are investigating the incident under Section 21(1) of the Police Act.

"Members of the public or witnesses with information are urged to come forward to assist investigations by contacting the Tun H.S. Lee Traffic Police Station at 03-2071 9999 or the nearest police station," he said.
Earlier, a dashcam video that went viral on social media showed an SUV attempting to follow the convoy before being noticed by one of the escorts, who was seen ordering the driver to stop.
The motorcycle escort was then seen speeding away after issuing the warning, while the SUV driver was seen accelerating towards the convoy in the right-most lane.
d54d08fd17568e11: PETALING JAYA: The government will study the feasibility of introducing residual payments or revenue sharing to ensure Malaysian actors benefit when works featuring their performances continue to generate commercial revenue.

Communications minister Fahmi Fadzil said his ministry, through the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas), will examine the suitability of introducing a residual payment or revenue-sharing mechanism for audiovisual works.
He said the review will consider whether such a mechanism should be implemented through amendments to the law, industry guidelines, or standard contracts.
It will also consider the structure of the creative industry ecosystem and current business models as well as practices adopted by streaming platforms and international distributors.
He was responding to Kalam Salan (PN-Sabak Bernam), who asked whether the government planned to introduce a residual payment or rerun royalty mechanism for actors.
Kalam said such a mechanism would allow actors to receive a reasonable share of profit generated when their work is used on television, in cinemas, on streaming platforms or in overseas markets.

Fahmi said that in the US, for example, residual payments are not specifically established by law, but are negotiated collectively between actors’ unions such as the Screen Actors Guild, the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists, and producers’ associations.
“Such payments are made to actors covered under the relevant agreements when a film or drama is used in markets after its initial release, including through television, video and streaming.

“For films, these payments are typically calculated as a percentage of the distributor’s gross receipts. The amount is then distributed among the actors based on their filming period and the original payment received by each actor,” he said in a written parliamentary reply.
In Malaysia, the Copyright Act 1987 provides certain rights to performers. However, there is currently no specific mechanism for residual payments for audiovisual works.
“Malaysian actors’ remuneration is generally determined based on the terms and conditions of contracts agreed between the actors and the producers or rights holders of the works,” Fahmi said.
Fahmi added that Finas will also work with the domestic trade and cost of living ministry as well as the Intellectual Property Corporation of Malaysia on the review exercise.

“The views of stakeholders will also be taken into account, including Gabungan Persatuan Karyawan Filem Malaysia, actors’ associations, and producers’ associations, to ensure that the mechanism developed takes into consideration the interests of all parties,” he said.
ea3fc27f05015ead: KUALA LUMPUR: Machang member of parliament Wan Ahmad Fayhsal Wan Ahmad Kamal has been hospitalised at Kuala Lumpur Hospital (HKL) after losing consciousness at home this morning.
He said he passed out while helping one of his children with homework.
"Earlier in the morning, while I was helping my child finish up some homework, I lost consciousness.
"I am now in HKL to undergo checks and emergency treatment. InsyaAllah, I will undergo a CT scan," he said in a social media posting.
Earlier, his private secretary, Wan Meor Safwat Naqiuddin Shamsudin, had said Wan Fayhsal was in stable condition in hospital.
ad6659143b54ffd0: Does it feel like people are perhaps a little grumpier or more on edge these days? It’s not like it’s without reason. There are wars. The climate is going haywire. Someone just died of plague. Scientific research is under attack. Machines keep stealing humans’ work. The media is a mess. And just when it all starts to feel a little overwhelming, Jaguar goes and unveils a new car.

The Type 01 is the first model to arrive from Jaguar’s rebirth. The British carmaker was an early entrant to the modern EV market with the 2017 I-Pace, which was fun to drive even if it was too small inside and perhaps completely unreliable. An all-electric sedan was supposed to be next, but a year from the showroom, it was abruptly canceled, leaving the automaker with nothing to sell as old models like the F-Pace ceased production.

Instead, Jaguar got to work on an all-new electric vehicle platform called JEA, which will underpin an all-electric product line. An elevated ownership experience and a starting price of about double the brand’s previous $60,000 entry point was the idea, Jaguar boss Rawdon Glover told me in 2024. Then last year the brand started teasing its relaunch, and everyone got upset. Things got even worse when the first images of the slab-sided and pastel-shaded Type 00 coupe concept leaked.
9141085d8af74295: KUALA LUMPUR: Congestion at the Bukit Bintang MRT station eased tonight after a surge in passenger numbers disrupted the flow of commuters on the Kajang Line around 8pm.
Rapid KL said in an update at 11pm that passenger movement at the station had returned to normal.
"We will continue to monitor the situation from time to time," it said in a statement, without elaborating on the cause of the congestion.
The congestion was also believed to have affected commuters at other stations, including Bangsar LRT station, where many passengers were left waiting.
A commuter, who wished to be known as AJ, said he had to wait for almost an hour at Bangsar LRT station while trying to get home to Meru, Klang.
AJ said station management had announced that trains had to be operated manually, slowing down services and resulting in more passengers waiting on the platform.
"The situation is still very crowded at Bangsar station and I have already missed 10 trains because I could not squeeze my way in.
"The frequency of trains appears to have returned to normal, with trains arriving every two minutes, but every train that arrives is packed with passengers," he said when contacted.
AJ expressed frustration over the recurring service disruptions and urged the rail operator to take proactive measures to address the issue.
He also called on the operator to take the problem seriously and avoid being complacent in dealing with recurring service disruptions.
9906349ea17892d9: PARIS: The International Energy Agency's member countries stand ready to release additional oil from their strategic reserves if necessary and will prioritise diesel due to tight supplies of the fuel, the head of the IEA said Wednesday.

IEA member states still have ample reserves of crude oil and refined products and stand "ready to release more of these stocks to the market if and when required," its director Fatih Birol said in a statement.

G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed last Friday to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the US-Iran war.

While shipments of crude through the Strait of Hormuz have recently picked up, damage to refineries in the region, along with those in Russia, have led to shortages of some refined products like diesel.
"IEA members also supported the prioritisation of the release of diesel stocks, to the extent possible, given the current tightness in diesel markets," Birol said in his statement.
The IEA said Saturday that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from 400 million barrels promised in March.
Birol said IEA member countries still have significant levels of publicly held emergency oil stocks – equivalent to around 1.1 billion barrels, including over 200 million barrels of diesel.
There have been concerns about the levels of oil reserves.
Saudi Aramco's chief executive Amin Nasser said Monday global oil stockpiles are "scarily thin" owing to the US-Iran war.
Nasser warned against looking at headline figures for reserves, noting that "less than 10%" were available.
A large portion of the reserves reported by countries represent the minimum volume required to keep infrastructure operational, he added.
6c38e6c94484033d: KUALA LUMPUR: Menteri Pertahanan Khaled Nordin menyangkal unjuran ketua audit negara bahawa kapal tempur pesisir pertama (LCS 1) hanya dijangka mula beroperasi pada Disember 2035.

Khaled berkata, tempoh masa dalam Laporan Ketua Audit Negara (LKAN) 2/2026 yang dikeluarkan pada Isnin itu berasaskan kontrak peluru berpandu dengan syarikat pertahanan Norway, Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, yang dibatalkan secara sepihak oleh negara itu.

Syarikat terbabit sebelum ini diberikan lanjutan masa atas 'sebab-sebab tertentu' memandangkan komponen peluru berpandu tersebut memerlukan kelulusan Washington, selain kekangan wabak Covid-19 yang turut menjejaskan jadual pelaksanaan, katanya.
Beliau berkata, LCS 1 sebaliknya berupaya memulakan operasi jauh lebih awal susulan langkah Malaysia meneroka perjanjian peluru berpandu alternatif dengan Korea Selatan, Turki dan Perancis.

“Tempoh penghantaran hanya ambil masa tiga tahun. Jadi kita sedang perhalus kesemua faktor ini, dan kita akan pastikan masa yang diambil untuk membekal serta memasang peluru berpandu itu tidak selama kontrak Norway.

“Justeru, berdasarkan faktor-faktor itu, (kami berpandangan) unjuran bahawa LCS 1 hanya siap pada Disember 2035 adalah tidak tepat dan tidak benar,” katanya ketika menggulung perbahasan LKAN bagi kementeriannya hari ini.
Khaled berkata, LCS itu tetap akan dilengkapi beberapa sistem persenjataan, walaupun belum dipasang dengan sistem peluru berpandu permukaan ke permukaan.
“Kapal ini masih dilengkapi peluru berpandu permukaan ke udara serta peluru berpandu permukaan ke laut bagi menyerang atau mematahkan sebarang ancaman kapal selam," katanya.
“Kita juga ada sistem peperangan elektromagnetik untuk menangani ancaman, selain sistem pengurusan tempur yang menyepadukan kesemua keupayaan ini dengan radar serta sistem penjejakan kapal."
Beliau turut menjelaskan, tentera udara boleh membantu menggempur sasaran yang lebih jauh bagi menampung ketiadaan sistem peluru berpandu permukaan ke permukaan berkenaan.
Malaysia kini menuntut ganti rugi lebih RM1 bilion daripada Kongsberg susulan tindakan Norway membatalkan permit eksport sistem peluru berpandu yang diperuntukkan bagi projek LCS itu.
Malaysia sebelum ini menempah sistem itu daripada Kongsberg di bawah kontrak 2018 bagi melengkapkan enam kapal LCS.
LKAN mendedahkan bahawa LCS 1 mungkin diserahkan tanpa persenjataan lengkap apabila siap pada Disember tahun ini, selain berkemungkinan hanya beroperasi sepenuhnya pada Disember 2035.

Laporan itu mendapati ujian percubaan dan pentauliahan bagi LCS 1 tidak dapat diselesaikan mengikut jadual, memandangkan lima kontrak pelengkap membabitkan sistem persenjataan serta sokongan masih belum selesai.
Audit terbabit turut mendapati setakat 25 Jun lalu, keseluruhan projek LCS mengalami kelewatan sebanyak 7.55% merangkumi kelima-lima kapal, dengan tempoh kelewatan antara 30 hingga 108 hari.
7503c47e3d9535c3: PETALING JAYA: Police arrested a 27-year-old man for allegedly tailing a police convoy escorting deputy prime minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on the Shah Alam Expressway (Kesas) this morning.
Kuala Lumpur traffic police chief Zamzuri Isa said the incident occurred at Km48.5 of the highway at about 9.30am as the convoy was travelling from Kajang to Sunway Medical Centre in Subang Jaya.
He said the driver of a Honda CR-V was warned by a police outrider against following the convoy but ignored him and continued to tailgate the convoy.
“The driver is believed to have continued following the convoy in a manner that could endanger the safety of the convoy and other road users,” Zamzuri said in a statement.
The driver was arrested and his vehicle was seized.
e0e668bdbe6651e6: PARIS: A remote island near Antarctica is no longer home to the world's largest penguin colony, as climate-driven changes to ocean food chains likely devastated its once-thriving inhabitants, a new study said Wednesday.

Drone and satellite images showed that the volcanic island of Zavodovski lost more than 680,000 – or two-thirds – of its chinstrap penguins between 2011 and 2025, according to the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).
"That's a very rapid loss," Norman Ratcliffe, the lead author of the BAS study published in the journal Current Biology, told AFP.
The study's findings raise concerns that chinstrap populations across the South Sandwich Islands, which include Zavodovski and are home to 38 percent of the species, have fallen.
The researchers suggest that the "alarming declines" should lead to chinstrap penguins being redesignated as "endangered" by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
This would be a sharp downgrade from their "least concern" classification, which means they are not currently threatened with extinction.
Surveys in 2011 had concluded that chinstrap populations across the South Sandwich Islands were stable.
But their number on Zavodovski fell from around 1.09 million breeding individuals in January 2011 to 402,000 in 2025, or a 63% decline, according to the study.
The island is also home to a different species, macaroni penguins, whose population rose from around 338,000 in 2011 to 433,000 in 2025 – and now outnumber chinstrap penguins.
Together, chinstraps and macaronis now total more than 835,000 on Zavodovski.
The researchers said the Adelie penguins of Cape Adare, on the other side of Antarctica, are now the world's largest penguin colony, numbering more than one million as of 2018.
Krill decline
Zavodovski island's Mount Curry volcano erupted in 2016, sparking fears that it could wipe out its penguin population.
But the researchers found that the ash cloud was blown northeast over an area not inhabited by the flightless birds.
"The decline in chinstrap colony area was in progress prior to the eruption and continued at a constant rate thereafter," the study said.
"We don't think the volcano is implicated or it's not the main driver (of the population decline) because what we see is a linear decline in the chinstrap penguins," Ratcliffe told AFP.
Instead, the scientists linked the drop in chinstrap numbers to a reduction in the availability of krill – the tiny shrimp-like creatures that are their main food source.
Warming ocean temperatures have pushed the crustaceans south toward colder waters, which chinstraps do not tolerate.
"We think that climate change operating through food webs is probably the main driver," Ratcliffe said.
The island's chinstrap population has been falling at a rate of seven percent per year.

Macaroni penguins have increased in number over the same period as they eat a wider range of prey than chinstraps. Their survival also supports the idea that the volcanic eruption was not a factor in the chinstrap's demise.

"The observed numerical shift from chinstraps to macaronis on Zavodovski represents the most striking change in penguin community composition that has been observed at a single location in Antarctica to date," the study said.

"The most plausible explanation for the observed patterns of population change is that a climate-induced regime shift has occurred that has been detrimental to the maritime Antarctic chinstraps but has favoured the subantarctic macaronis."
c9d6ca5ec47f0687: PETALING JAYA: Bersama has unveiled its shadow federal budget, which includes the reintroduction of the goods and services tax (GST) capped at a 5% rate and the abolition of several cash aid schemes in favour of more targeted monthly assistance.
The party said capping the GST at 5% for the next 10 years would provide certainty for households and businesses, while containing the impact of the tax scheme on future inflation.

“Based on Bersama’s estimates, a 5% GST could generate approximately RM76.1 billion in revenue in 2027, or 3.3% of the GDP, compared with the RM59.4 billion expected to be collected through the (6%) sales and service tax in 2026.
“This would generate additional revenue of approximately RM16.7 billion,” the party said in its shadow budget.
Bersama proposed scrapping the Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) and Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) schemes and replacing them with a distribution of RM200 a month to the bottom 60% of households (B60).
It also proposed that every Malaysian child under 18 receive RM50 a month, capped at five children per household, for a maximum benefit of RM250 a month or RM3,000 a year per household.
Bersama also said the government should study the possibility of implementing a retail electronic payment tax (REPT) from 2027 to 2029.
“No REPT will be imposed during the development period. Subject to the feasibility of the framework, REPT could be introduced in 2030 at a rate of 0.5%,” it said.
“REPT at a rate of 0.5% on this base could potentially generate about RM9.1 billion a year, before taking into account exemptions and behavioural changes."
It said these measures could, among others, help Malaysia eliminate its fiscal deficit and record its first budget surplus since 1997 by 2035.
92e0f551fb2a5298: GUA MUSANG: Two men were injured after being slashed with a sword during a fight at a rubber store at Rancangan Pemulihan Tanah (RPT) Kesedar Sungai Terah yesterday.
The incident, which occurred at 8.30pm, was believed to have stemmed from a dispute over the disposal of broken mosaic tiles and damage to a closed-circuit television (CCTV) camera at the store.

Gua Musang police chief Superintendent Sik Choon Foo said preliminary investigations found that the incident occurred during a discussion where a 27-year-old man allegedly tried to pull out a sword tucked behind his back.
"One of the victims tried to stop him, leading to a struggle. The suspect then swung the sword.
"As a result, the first victim, 33, suffered an 18cm cut to his left cheek, while the second victim, 40, sustained a 5cm cut to his right arm," he said when contacted.
He said one of the injured men was still receiving treatment at a hospital.
Sik said the suspect tried to flee after the incident but was detained by members of the public before being handed over to police.
"Police also seized a sword with a wooden sheath and a knife to assist investigations.
"The case is being investigated under Section 326 of the Penal Code for voluntarily causing grievous hurt with a dangerous weapon," he said.
b7f6469a00a13afd: HONG KONG: Hong Kong arrested nine people in a city-wide operation targeting illicit fuel activities, authorities said on Wednesday, as surging global oil prices continue to put pressure on the import-dependent financial hub.
The city lacks its own refineries and imports its entire supply of automotive fuel, with much of it coming from neighbouring mainland China.
Prices at Hong Kong's filling stations are among the world's most expensive, creating a growing incentive for smugglers to transport cheaper fuel illegally across the border into the city.
Authorities said they seized more than 30,000 litres of smuggled fuel worth more than HK$1 million (US$127,000) in September, arresting eight men and one woman.

Criminals are using modified cross-boundary trucks or private cars with enlarged fuel tanks to smuggle fuel through control points, Chong Sin-han, a senior investigator at the customs department, told reporters on Wednesday.
"Fuel prices remain persistently high, tempting illegal traders to sell more untaxed gasoline for profit and tempting citizens to take risks by purchasing it," said Chong.
Authorities seized vehicles that "were unventilated, increasing the risk of fire or explosion", said Leung Nam-cheuk, a fire officer at the anti-illicit fuelling activities task force.

The retail price of standard petrol reached about HK$34.60 per litre in Hong Kong this week, which saw a jump of 16.6 per cent since late February as the Middle East conflict disrupts global shipping and strains energy supplies.

Hong Kong also saw rises in freight and insurance costs, which pushed diesel prices to record highs, authorities told lawmakers on Wednesday, noting the Strait of Hormuz shipping routes faced significant disruptions and that Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure came under renewed attacks.
As of September, Hong Kong customs officials had arrested at least 84 people suspected of engaging in illegal fuel dealings this year and seized 95,000 litres of fuel.--AFP
5ccd4588ad9e86bc: SINGAPORE: Singapore is set to fall short of its 2035 target of importing 6 gigawatts of low-carbon electricity, a report from research and consultancy firm Wood Mackenzie said on Wednesday.
The country has approved 9.25 GW of import capacity across six corridors, but none of the projects has reached financial close or begun construction, the report added.
Here are the key points from the report:

Singapore generates up to 95 per cent of its electricity from natural gas. By 2035, imported green power is likely to be at 15 per cent of its power generation mix, roughly half of EMA's target of about one-third of projected demand at 6 GW.
Key obstacles include export permit regimes, project bankability, cross-border transmission financing and the lack of a mechanism for buyers to claim the carbon value of imported power.
Malaysia is the only corridor with a credible path to delivery this decade through an existing interconnector with up to 1 GW of capacity.
EMA approved 900 MW of imports from Johor, in August, including 300 MW for Sembcorp Utilities that could begin supplying power by 2029.
Sarawak, which has secured a cable supplier, is realistically targeting commercial operation in the mid-2030s.
Indonesia accounts for 37 per cent of the approved pipeline, but progress has stalled due to export permit requirements and local-content rules.
Vietnam, Cambodia and Australia together account for 43 per cent of the pipeline, though all remain at the conditional approval stage with no visible construction timeline.
Imported power must compete with Singapore's wholesale electricity price, while EMA has also expanded plans for hydrogen-ready gas-fired generation.--REUTERS
72b30c0bd9203af0: As drums pounded and chants rang out, 16-year-old Yanis, flanked by a knot of friends, rattled off why he had joined tens of thousands surging through the streets of Paris on Tuesday to demand better learning conditions.
"There are no toilets, no toilet paper, everything is broken," he said, his schoolmates nodding and chiming in.
"We go to class from 8am to 6pm with a one-hour break."
"There are 36 of us in class. We can't study," the teenager from the northern Paris suburb of Sarcelles said, calling conditions at his high school "unacceptable".
He was among some 56,000 people who poured onto the streets of Paris on Tuesday as part of a protest movement that began in late September.

Across France, students and teachers have blocked entrances to hundreds of high schools for 15- to 17-year-olds, protesting against teacher shortages, overloaded timetables, ill-equipped classrooms and buildings not designed to cope with rising temperatures.
On Tuesday, protesters flooded into the Place de la Republique in central Paris, hoisting signs.
"2026 is the new 1789," declared one, a nod to the French Revolution.
Another placard took the form of an oversized middle finger.
The scent of merguez sausages — a fixture of French demonstrations —drifted through the square.
Demonstrators danced and clapped to pounding drums, breaking into chants calling for President Emmanuel Macron to resign and denouncing the far right ahead of presidential elections next year.
But beneath the festive atmosphere, some of young protesters struck a bleaker note.
Fidele, 15, who had come with Yanis, dreamt of becoming a lawyer, but said conditions at his school had left him pessimistic about whether he could get there.
"When I see the system, I tell myself that I don't have a future" in this country, he said.
Nearby, 16-year-old Noham has his sights set on becoming a computer engineer, but worried that overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages were putting that ambition out of reach.
"Without access to an education, I can't have the job I dream of," he said.
"It's an enormous amount of stress."
Nadine Zilliacus, an educator for 20 years, said she has seen the same disillusionment take hold among even younger pupils, who increasingly express a "really dark" view of what lies ahead.
"We tell them you have to prepare for the future with a job you like," she said.
"Even in middle school, they tell us: 'There's no point anyway. We won't have jobs'."
Further along the route, the crowd pressed towards the march's endpoint, clapping and chanting before voices swelled into a rendition of Marseille, France's national anthem.
From a balcony overhead, a silver-haired woman leaned out to encourage protesters below.
Spotting her, the crowd turned their faces upwards and broke into chants of "Mamie! Mamie!" — an affectionate French term for grandmother.
Among those making their way through the crowd was Ami, 17, who travelled into Paris with a group of friends to protest against conditions at her high school in the city's suburbs.
"Compared with schools in central Paris, we're neglected."
As the march reached the Nation roundabout, the festive mood began to shift, with police carrying riot shields barring the route and some protesters throwing stones at officers.
As Ami and her friends drew closer, the boom of tear gas canisters fired by police cut through the singing. The girls screamed and stopped in their tracks, unsure whether to keep moving forward.
Nearby, a middle-aged woman had mascara streaking down her face after being caught in the tear gas, while a young man comforted her.
Ami said she did not understand the police response.
"We're just protesting, we're singing and that's all," she said, adding that she was scared.
After a day of drums, chants and dancing through the capital, she was ready to leave.
"We just want to go home."

80efd5d11e6f899f: One of Donald Trump’s biggest goals as president is to increase domestic manufacturing and reshore supply chains so that the most in-demand technologies in the world can be 100 percent made in the United States.

By executive order last December, he launched his “Genesis Mission,” an ambitious plan seeking to leverage US dominance in AI to maintain or seize an edge in advanced robotics, biotechnology, semiconductors, and nuclear technologies. According to Trump, that plan works best with self-sustaining supply chains. Not even neighboring countries or longtime allies should be relied upon to manufacture a single component of any US product in his ideal world.

The Consumer Technology Association (CTA) has long warned that Trump’s reshoring goals are not grounded in reality, but only recently has America’s largest technology trade association attempted to estimate what it would cost businesses and consumers to follow through on Trump’s plan.

959d3472deaa6f96: LONDON: Andy Burnham needs to win over voters like tech worker Dani Arbid in a by-election on Thursday if he is to fend off a national threat to his Labour Party from the Greens — and the early signs are encouraging for Britain's new prime minister.

The vote for a parliamentary seat in the inner London electoral district of Holborn and St Pancras, made vacant by the resignation of former prime minister Keir Starmer, is a first test of whether Burnham can restore voters' faith in Labour, which saw its popularity among left-wing voters plunge over the war in Gaza.

Many, like Arbid, turned instead to the Greens, helping them to their strongest result ever in local elections in May. Now, he says he is undecided on how he will vote in Thursday's so-called by-election but welcomed Burnham's tougher messaging on Israel and his more ambitious approach to ties with the European Union.

"It's very important to read the room, which I think the current Labour government is doing a lot better job at," Arbid, 38, told Reuters. "There is still room for Labour to kind of claw back some of those losses for sure."

Unlike the national picture, where Nigel Farage's Reform UK poses a serious challenge to Burnham, the by-election is mainly a contest between Labour and the Greens, with thousands of activists from both parties out canvassing in recent weeks.

Burnham hopes to show he can consolidate the left-of-centre vote, strengthening his efforts to take on a British right now split between Reform UK and the Conservatives. But the by-election also offers him a chance to rob the Greens of the momentum they have built up under new leader Zack Polanski.
Polanski himself is the Greens' candidate in Holborn and St Pancras but Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, a local council leader, is tipped to hold the seat for the governing party.

Green gains in areas of London contributed to Labour's dismal local election results in May, which helped set in train a process that culminated on July 20 with Starmer's resignation and his replacement by Burnham.
Since then, however, Labour has rebounded in national opinion polls, while the Greens have suffered setbacks.

At a conference last weekend, Green Party members voted to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jewish groups, Israel and even some Green lawmakers. Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote.
Burnham's government, which has taken a more critical approach towards Israel and banned the import of goods from West Bank settlements, said the Greens had overstepped a line.

On Camden High Street, an area of London brimming with market stalls and popular with musicians, artists and tourists, Kamran Ahmed, a local resident who works in AI, said Polanski could have managed the issues raised at conference better.

But on a local level he said the Greens had something new to offer, echoing frustration heard around the country that the previously dominant Conservative and Labour parties no longer have the answers.

"Nothing is set in stone, but some of the mainstream parties have over-promised and under-delivered... If you take an area like Camden, it could benefit from some of the fresher thinking that the Green Party offers," Ahmed said.

Damian Lyons Lowe, head of pollster Survation, said the seat was one of the Greens' top targets, and that governments rarely did well at by-elections. But the Greens' anti-Starmer message, which resonated so well in May, was being tested by Burnham.
"Burnham has made direct appeals to Green-minded voters in terms of some of the things they care about," he told Reuters.
"The Burnham vibe check is very different to the Starmer-led Labour government, and that's a problem for the Green Party."
