b98b256615530f54: COLOMBO: Sri Lanka's anti-graft authority arrested former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa on Wednesday over allegations that her charity misused donations collected for a children's hospital, dealing a major blow to the once powerful family.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake's government has revived long-dormant graft investigations involving members of the once-powerful Rajapaksa family, which dominated Sri Lankan politics for nearly two decades.
The 73-year-old wife of former president Mahinda was remanded in custody until Tuesday by a Colombo magistrate.
She was arrested earlier in the day by the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) which questioned her for nearly seven hours.

"The magistrate ordered her to be held in custody till Oct 13 and to admit her to the prison hospital because of an eye condition," a court official told reporters outside the Colombo Magistrate's Court.
In another development, a Rajapaksa-era foreign minister, Rohitha Bogollagama, was also arrested Wednesday for corruption.
The Colombo High Court ordered the 72-year-old Bogollagama to be held in custody till the end of a trial against him for misusing state funds in 2006 when he was minister of investment promotion.

The former first lady was arrested in connection with an investigation into her Siriliya Saviya Foundation, which had raised money to buy equipment for hospitals, including a children's cancer facility.
Her lawyer, Manoj Gamage, told reporters that she denied the allegations made against her and will contest the charges of misappropriating donations raised for charity.
The CIABOC also arrested the former head of a state-owned bank after accusing him of giving 10 million rupees (US$30,000) to her charity, the agency said.
Pradeep Kariyawasam, the then-chairman of the National Savings Bank was released on bail.
- FAMILY UNDER SIEGE -
Shiranthi Rajapaksa travelled to Singapore on Sept 16 for medical treatment, and was served with a summons at Colombo airport to provide a statement to police about her charity.
She flew back on Monday after filing a court petition seeking to prevent her arrest, but the hearing for anticipatory bail was fixed for Oct 12.
Police said the authorities wanted to question Shiranthi Rajapaksa over the donations collected by her charity for a scanner intended for a cancer hospital for children.
Investigators told a court that the scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government, but the charity allegedly continued to solicit donations and misused the funds.
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing, saying the money had not been misappropriated.
Other members of the family have also faced legal troubles.
The former first lady's eldest son, opposition lawmaker Namal Rajapaksa, is in remand custody over allegations linked to a 2013 Airbus aircraft deal signed during his father's presidency.
The Rajapaksa family has consistently denied the corruption allegations and dismissed the cases against them as politically motivated.

Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president from 2005 to 2015 and remains one of Sri Lanka's most influential political figures, despite the decline in the family's fortunes since mass protests ousted his brother, Gotabaya Rajapaksa, from the presidency in 2022.--AFP

78d51e3487b8191e: If you think all the new investment spending pouring into the world economy right now is solely targeted at Big Tech and artificial intelligence, you're only half right.
According to some estimates, the planned increase in Group of Seven (G7) defence spending over the next decade may match it — even if the overlap between the two is now huge.

Another measure of the simultaneous stimulus to global economic activity and inflation — alongside pressure on public purses and rising borrowing rates—is the eye-popping scale of planned defence spending over the coming decade.

Former United States Navy Admiral James Stavridis, now managing director and partner at The Carlyle Group, estimated this week that additional defence commitments from G7 governments over the next 10 years will amount to some US$8 trillion of additional re-armament spending on top of prior trends.

With the collective annual gross domestic product (GDP) now just over US$55 trillion for the US, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada, an US$8 trillion increase over a decade amounts to almost 15 per cent of 2026's GDP.
Stavridis points out that G7 defence spending has risen to two per cent of GDP, its highest share in more than 30 years, with that share projected to rise to 3.8 per cent as soon as 2030.

Across Europe alone, he said, broader defence goals imply roughly €4 trillion to €5 trillion of additional spending over the coming decade —rising towards €9 trillion "when adjacent infrastructure is included".
The earmarked increase in US defence outlays in the 2027 fiscal year to a record US$1.5 trillion would surpass the World War 2 peak in inflation-adjusted dollars.

According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates, that level of defence spending by then would amount to some 4.6 per cent of the US GDP —just shy of 2009's peaks and approaching levels last seen at the height of the Cold War in the 1980s.

That budget boost may bring the US defence bill back above the current estimate for annual Treasury debt servicing costs — although at the rate at which bond yields are rising, there could be a protracted race between the two to gobble up US tax dollars.

The main point Stavridis makes is that this spending is likely to be very different in terms of procurement than in the past—far less on warships and tanks and more on tech, drones, cybersecurity and battlefield AI.

"The centre of gravity is moving towards smaller, faster-moving companies in cyber, encryption and hypersonics rather than the traditional prime contractors, and the deals being struck are correspondingly smaller and more numerous," he wrote.
Data centres and their security are another common factor between both.

This is nowhere more salient than in Europe, where the Russian threat to Europe's eastern borders, doubts about US commitment to the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation under President Donald Trump and a ratcheting up of defence spending across the continent combine in ways that some hope will also boost its tech sector.

"Two decades of declining European defence investment tracked closely with two decades of declining European tech competitiveness, a pattern the current rearmament cycle appears determined to reverse," Stavridis noted.
All of which will be cold comfort for restive government bond markets having to absorb the additional borrowing that goes with these increases.
The defence-to-debt-servicing ratio has historically been cited as a warning metric signalling debt sustainability concerns.

The Washington-based Institute of International Finance recently estimated that average government borrowing costs across the G7 are now at their highest since mid-2008, while annual interest expenses are nearly 85 per cent higher.

Over the past year, advanced economies paid more than US$ 3.3 trillion in interest on internationally traded government bonds alone —more than the estimated US$2.6 trillion of global spending on AI, US$3.1 trillion on defence or US$2.3 trillion on clean energy.
The sheer scale of economic stimulus from both the defence and AI splurges may be at least reining in debt-to-GDP ratios.
But there's little doubt that the world's major economies are now entering a high-octane, highstakes balancing act that may achieve its goals but risks increasing instability in the process.
No one is fully sure where this all ends.
The writer is from Reuters

aaec9f447bd4f40a: BANGKOK: Ex-Thai premier Thaksin Shinawatra told a court on Wednesday that his life could be in danger if authorities seize assets including bullet-proof vehicles as part of a US$500 million, decades-old tax dispute.

The Supreme Court's Tax Division last November upheld a tax claim by the Revenue Department against the former prime minister – one of Thailand's richest people – over the 2006 sale of his telecoms firm.

Thaksin has sought a temporary injunction against the Revenue Department to stop it from seizing his assets to pay the bill, which his lawyer Winyat Chatmontree told AFP was worth more than 17 billion baht (US$504 million).

"I am not sure if someone intends to harm me," Thaksin said, adding that if his cars were taken, "what if my life is in danger? Who will take responsibility?"
Thaksin also argued that he has already settled the bill for the tax-free sale of Shin Corp to Singapore's Temasek Holdings.
The 2006 deal, which netted the Shinawatra family a US$1.9-billion windfall, sparked protests and became a lightning rod for opposition to Thaksin's populist government.
He was ousted in a coup later that year and went into exile for more than a decade, during which time he was convicted of corruption.
When he returned in 2023, Thaksin was arrested but sent to hospital and then freed. He finally saw the inside of a jail last year, serving eight months before his release in May.
The tax court is due to deliver its ruling on Nov 16.
The Shinawatra clan has for two decades been the key foe of Thailand's pro-military, pro-royalty elite, who view their populist brand of politics as a threat to the traditional social order.

But the Shinawatra dynasty has faced a series of legal and political setbacks, including the court-ordered removal of Thaksin's daughter, Paetongtarn, as prime minister in August 2025 over an ethics breach.--AFP

07f91cfa576c78b5: Receiving suspected scam calls is almost an everyday event for Malaysians now. News of victims who fell for such scams and in the process lost money in the tens or hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of ringgit have become commonplace as well.

It used to be that unsuspecting Malaysians regularly fell for job offers that were too good to be true in neighbouring countries, only to be forced into the unsavoury task of swindling other people of their cash.

After recent high-profile crackdowns on such scam operations in places like Cambodia, the perpetrators seem to be on the move. Malaysia is in their sights but it is most reassuring that the authorities are on alert and on the lookout.
Police have just identified a rented villa in rural Melaka where 11 Japanese as well as four Chinese and two Myanmar citizens were arrested and the usual scam operation paraphernalia seized.

The syndicate operating this centre is said to be targeting victims in Japan. And at an abandoned resort in Pahang , the Immigration Department netted 98 people, 95 of whom are foreigners, suspected of being members of another scam-call syndicate.

Scam centres are changing, moving across international borders and trying to blend into out-of-the-way locales in order to avoid detection. Our crime-busters must, therefore, be quick to stay ahead of these syndicates as well.
The above two raids prove that our enforcement agencies are capable of tracking increasingly sophisticated syndicates. However, one or two busted operations do not mean the problem is under control.

Scam operators are proving highly adaptable, mobile and increasingly technology-enabled. When one location becomes too hot, they move — sometimes across borders, sometimes just a few hours away from the city.

The authorities must be equally adaptable and need to stay ahead rather than merely respond after the fact. Vigilance must extend beyond traditional hotspots to seemingly quiet, remote and abandoned properties.
Ordinary Malaysians must also be alert and quickly report any suspicious movements and activities in their midst.
These are highly lucrative illegal operations and the operators can be counted on to be highly creative as well in order to avert getting caught.
There is, therefore, no room for complacency and resting on the laurels of a few busted operations.

There must be no let-up in hunting down such operations wherever and whenever they sprout up. Every dismantled operation should also provide invaluable clues and intelligence to assist in identifying the next one.
Enforcement agencies, local authorities, property owners and the community at large must all remain alert to unusual activity. The syndicates are constantly changing their playbook.
Malaysia needs to do the same to get a step or two ahead of them. A whole-of-society approach is required to tackle this menace.
5d7fcd4649aa4de4: Training the largest AI models is no longer simply a question of adding more GPUs. As clusters grow, power availability is becoming a hard physical constraint, forcing infrastructure teams to consider how a single training workload can operate across multiple data centres. That creates a very different networking problem. Traditional datacenter interconnect was designed to move traffic between sites. AI training demands something more exacting: huge, synchronous flows, minimal packet loss and tightly coordinated communication between GPUs. If one part of the cluster stalls, the impact can ripple across the entire job. In this interview, The Register’s Tim Phillips speaks with Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon and Systems Architecture, Cisco Fellow, about what Cisco calls the “Scale-Across” imperative and why it believes distributed AI infrastructure requires a new approach to routing. Rakesh explains how the demands of AI are changing the role of the network, from simple transport to an integral part of the compute system. He discusses the challenge of making geographically separate facilities behave more like a single deterministic machine, and why buffering, high-speed coherent optics and tightly integrated silicon matter when workloads span long-distance fiber links. The conversation also looks inside the cluster itself. Rakesh outlines how Cisco’s Silicon One architecture and Intelligent Collective Networking are designed to manage synchronized bursts of GPU traffic, reduce bottlenecks and improve job completion time. Power efficiency is another central theme, including the trade-off between network consumption and the energy available to GPUs. Security and longevity also come into focus. The interview covers hardware-accelerated MACsec and IPsec, as well as the role of programmability in helping infrastructure adapt as AI workloads continue to evolve. For infrastructure and datacenter leaders planning for larger, more distributed AI environments, the discussion offers a practical view of the networking challenges that emerge once one site is no longer enough. b999265e92671415: KUALA LUMPUR: Defence minister Khaled Nordin has rubbished the auditor-general's projection that the first littoral combat ship (LCS 1) may only commence operations in December 2035.

Khaled said this timeframe in the Auditor-General's Report 2/2026 released on Monday was based on the missile contract with Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, which was unilaterally scrapped by Norway.
The firm had been given time extensions due to "certain reasons" as components of the missiles required approval by Washington, while the Covid-19 pandemic had also affected the timeframe, he said.
He said the LCS 1 would be able to start operations much earlier now that Malaysia was seeking alternative missile deals with Korea, Turkey and France.

"The delivery time would be just three years. So we are weighing all of these factors, and we will ensure that the time it would take to deliver and install the missiles would not be as long as the Norway contract.

"Therefore, we believe that, based on these factors, the projection of the LCS 1 being completed in December 2035 is inaccurate and untrue," he said when winding up the debate on the A-G's report for his ministry today.
Khaled said the LCS would still be armed with several weapons systems, although not with a surface-to-surface missile system yet.
"It will still be equipped with surface-to-air missiles as well as surface-to-sea missiles to attack or counter any threat from submarines.
"We also have electromagnetic war systems to counter threats and a combat management system that integrates all these capabilities with the ship's radar and tracking systems," he said.
He also said the air force could help take on targets further away in the absence of the surface-to-surface missile system.
Malaysia is seeking more than RM1 billion in compensation from Kongsberg after Norway revoked its export permit for the missile system meant for the LCS.
Malaysia ordered the system from Kongsberg under a 2018 contract to equip six LCS vessels.
The A-G’s report said the LCS 1 could be handed over unarmed when completed in December this year, and that it may only be fully operational in December 2035.
It found that trials and commissioning for the LCS 1 could not be completed on schedule, with five complementary contracts for weapons and support systems still incomplete.
The audit also found that as of June 25, the overall LCS project was 7.55% behind schedule across all five ships, with delays ranging from 30 to 108 days.

6f33a116fc3c3db5: GAZA CITY: Israel carried out new strikes in Gaza on Wednesday as it marked the third anniversary of the Oct 7 attacks by Hamas, with Palestinian officials reporting three people dead.
Loud bangs across the border in Gaza were audible from the site of the Nova music festival just as family members gathered at dawn to mourn the more than 300 revellers killed three years earlier.
In Gaza City, Al-Shifa hospital reported two people killed in an Israeli strike overnight.
Gaza's civil defence identified one of the dead as Mohamed Tamous and said he was a volunteer for the agency, which serves as an emergency rescue service under Hamas.

The Israeli military said it struck and killed "two Hamas terrorists who had exited Kamal Adwan Hospital in the northern Gaza Strip," adding that one had "planted explosives... in the area of the Yellow Line with the intention of harming IDF troops."
The so-called Yellow Line demarcates the areas under Hamas and Israeli military control in the Gaza Strip.
The military identified one of those killed in the strike as Tamous, whom it said was a sniper in Hamas's military wing while simultaneously working for the civil defence.
In the southern city of Khan Younis, Nasser Hospital said that a 60-year-old man, Hisham Ibrahim Abu Mustafa, was killed in an Israeli strike and that others were injured.

On the third anniversary of the first day of the war in Gaza, living conditions remain dire in the coastal Palestinian territory, despite a US-brokered ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025.
"After three years of siege, killing and destruction, Israel has turned the Gaza Strip into an uninhabitable place," said Gaza City resident Mahmoud Abu Hasira.
Hundreds of thousands of displaced people still live in tent cities and makeshift shelters that sprawl on beaches or next to piles of rubble from bombed-out residential buildings.

"We once had homes, but now we have lost our loved ones, whose bodies still lie beneath the rubble," said Bassam Nasser, a resident of Beit Hanoun, a now largely destroyed city in Gaza's north, who was displaced in the early days of the war.
Israel says it controls about 60 percent of Gaza, on the territory's outer perimeter including Beit Hanoun, while most of the Palestinian population lives in the remaining Hamas-controlled areas.
Though Israel eased its restrictions on aid trucks entering Gaza after the ceasefire, Ahmed Nasser, another resident of Gaza City, told AFP that life remained desperately hard.
"The war and the famine have left us hungry, fearful and displaced, living in tents and struggling with soaring prices," he said.

Israel's military offensive has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Since the ceasefire was declared last October, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,460 people in Gaza, according to the ministry.
bfc56202ebcf1477: PUTRAJAYA: The Court of Appeal today upheld a retired policeman's 12-year prison sentence and two strokes of the rotan for sexually assaulting a five-year-old girl whom his daughter had been babysitting.
A three-member bench comprising judges Datuk Azman Abdullah, K. Muniandy and Dean Wayne Daly dismissed the 76-year-old man's appeal against his conviction and sentence.
Azman said there was overwhelming and convincing evidence, notwithstanding that the victim was eight years old when she gave evidence.
He said her testimony remained consistent with the contents of the police report lodged by her father and the medical report.
He said the heinous act had not only left the victim with physical injuries but had also caused her deep psychological distress.
"The law exists as a bastion of justice to protect the weak. In this case, the victim is a child who was incapable of resisting or fully comprehending what the appellant did to her," he said.

Azman said the sentence imposed was intended to serve as a reminder not only to the appellant but also to the general public that age does not confer a licence upon any person to act with impunity towards a child.
The court issued a warrant of committal for the man to commence his sentence from today.

The man, who was present in court in a wheelchair, had previously been granted a stay of execution of his sentence and bail of RM10,000 with one surety pending disposal of his appeal, which was heard today.
Azman said the execution of the whipping conviction would be determined by the prison authorities based on whether or not he is fit to undergo the sentence.
Earlier, lawyer Mohd Rusnizam Abdullah told the court that his client had met with an accident and his health had deteriorated.
On April 19, 2024, the Kuantan Sessions Court found the man guilty of sexual assaulting the victim at a house in Kuantan in 2020.
He was sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment and two strokes of the rotan. The High Court upheld the Sessions Court's decision on Jan 27 this year.

At today's proceedings, Mohd Rusnizam argued that the victim was not competent to testify because she did not fully understand the implications of giving truthful evidence and the consequences of lying.
Deputy Public Prosecutor Jasmee Hameeza Jaafar, however, submitted that the victim was a competent witness as she remembered vividly what had happened.
e53194ec5f1b977c: KUALA LUMPUR: The Communications Ministry, through the National Film Development Corporation Malaysia (Finas), will study the residual payment or revenue-sharing mechanism for audiovisual works in Malaysia.

Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said the study would take into account three main aspects, namely legislation, the structure of the creative industry ecosystem and current business models, and the practices of streaming platforms and international distributors.
"The study will examine whether the mechanism should be implemented through amendments to existing laws, industry guidelines or standard contracts," he said in a parliamentary written reply today.
He was responding to Kalam Salan (PN-Sabak Bernam) on whether the government planned to introduce a residual payment or rerun royalty mechanism for Malaysian actors.
Fahmi said Finas would work with the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry and the Intellectual Property Corporation of Malaysia.
He said the mechanism could ensure actors continued to receive reasonable economic benefits when works featuring their performances were commercially exploited after their initial release.
He said this included through television reruns, streaming platforms and international markets.
Fahmi said the Copyright Act 1987 currently provided certain rights to performers.
"However, there is currently no specific mechanism for residual payments for audiovisual works.
"Actors' remuneration is generally determined based on the terms and conditions agreed between the actors and producers or rights holders," he said.

Fahmi said the views of stakeholders would also be taken into account, including the Federation of Malaysian Film Industry Workers Associations, actors' associations and producers' associations, to ensure the proposed mechanism considered the interests of all parties.
e8cac8c90ee44891: KUALA LUMPUR: Lapan Ahli Parlimen kerajaan hari ini menerima memorandum daripada kumpulan alam sekitar, Greenpeace Malaysia, yang menggesa tindakan diambil terhadap syarikat-syarikat Malaysia yang dinamakan dalam penemuan mengenai firma yang didakwa mempunyai kaitan dengan jerebu rentas sempadan.

Ahli Parlimen berkenaan ialah Dr Kelvin Yii (Bandar Kuching), Young Syefura Othman (Bentong), Khoo Poay Tiong (Kota Melaka), Syerleena Abdul Rashid (Bukit Bendera), R Yuneswaran (Segamat), Tan Kar Hing (Gopeng), Tan Hong Pin (Bakri) dan Hassan Karim (Pasir Gudang).

Memorandum itu susulan penemuan Greenpeace Indonesia, Greenpeace Malaysia dan Pantau Gambut yang mengenal pasti 20 syarikat yang didakwa mempunyai kaitan dengan titik panas kebakaran di Indonesia, termasuk firma yang mempunyai kaitan dengan Malaysia dan Singapura.

Greenpeace Malaysia menggesa kerajaan mengambil tindakan terhadap syarikat yang terbukti bertanggungjawab, mempercepatkan cadangan undang-undang jerebu rentas sempadan serta mendapatkan ketelusan lebih tinggi daripada Indonesia berhubung lokasi kebakaran, hasil siasatan dan syarikat yang berpotensi mempunyai kaitan dengan kebakaran berkenaan.
Syerleena berkata jerebu telah menjadi masalah berulang yang menjejaskan kualiti udara, sekolah dan kesihatan awam. "Kita sudah tahu puncanya. Kini kita memerlukan tindakan," katanya.
Beliau menggesa Malaysia, Singapura dan Indonesia bekerjasama sebagai negara tetangga Asean untuk menangani masalah itu, selain kerjasama antara masyarakat sivil, Parlimen dan kerajaan.
Yii pula berkata langkah sedia ada seperti pemantauan, perkongsian data dan pembenihan awan tidak mencukupi dan hanya memberikan kelegaan jangka pendek.

Katanya, beliau pada 6 Okt mengemukakan soalan Parlimen kepada Kementerian Sumber Asli dan Kelestarian Alam mengenai kesiapsiagaan Malaysia menghadapi jerebu serta kemungkinan memperkenalkan undang-undang pencemaran jerebu rentas sempadan.
Yii berkata kementerian menyatakan terdapat kesukaran mendapatkan bukti, menjalankan siasatan dan menguatkuasakan undang-undang terhadap pihak di luar bidang kuasa Malaysia.
"Kekangan ini tidak seharusnya dijadikan alasan untuk kita tidak mengambil tindakan tegas," katanya.
Beliau menggesa cadangan undang-undang itu dibawa ke jawatankuasa pilihan khas Parlimen supaya Ahli Parlimen dapat berusaha merangka undang-undang yang berkesan dan boleh dikuatkuasakan.
Yii turut menggesa Malaysia membangkitkan isu itu pada mesyuarat Asean akan datang dan mendesak tindakan lebih tegas di bawah perjanjian Asean mengenai pencemaran jerebu rentas sempadan.

Khoo pula berkata beliau telah mengemukakan usul kepada speaker Dewan Rakyat bagi membahaskan isu jerebu, yang disifatkannya sebagai krisis nasional yang menjejaskan kesihatan awam, keselamatan, ekonomi dan kesejahteraan rakyat.
Beliau turut berkata syarikat Malaysia perlu dikenakan tindakan tegas jika didapati terlibat dalam kebakaran di Indonesia.

"Undang-undang sedia ada mesti digunakan terhadap mereka. Jika tiada undang-undang yang terpakai, kerajaan perlu mengeluarkan amaran keras dan mengambil langkah lain, seperti menyenaraihitamkan atau memboikot syarikat berkenaan, jika boleh," katanya.

37a5dad272b4c009: KUALA LUMPUR: Eight government MPs today received a memorandum from environmental group Greenpeace Malaysia calling for action against Malaysian companies named in findings on firms allegedly linked to the transboundary haze.

The MPs are Dr Kelvin Yii (Bandar Kuching), Young Syefura Othman (Bentong), Khoo Poay Tiong (Kota Melaka), Syerleena Abdul Rashid (Bukit Bendera), R Yuneswaran (Segamat), Tan Kar Hing (Gopeng), Tan Hong Pin (Bakri) and Hassan Karim (Pasir Gudang).

The memorandum followed findings by Greenpeace Indonesia, Greenpeace Malaysia and Pantau Gambut, which identified 20 companies allegedly linked to fire hotspots in Indonesia. They include Malaysian and Singaporean-linked firms.

Greenpeace Malaysia called on the government to take action against those companies proven to be responsible, expedite a proposed transboundary haze law, and seek greater transparency from Indonesia on fire locations, investigation findings, and companies potentially linked to the fires.
Syerleena said the haze had become a recurring problem, affecting air quality, schools and public health. “We already know the cause. Now we need action,” she said.
She called on Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia to work together as Asean neighbours to tackle the problem, alongside cooperation between civil society, Parliament and governments.
Yii said existing measures such as monitoring, data sharing, and cloud seeding were insufficient and only provided short-term relief.

He said he had submitted a parliamentary question to the natural resources and environmental sustainability ministry on Oct 6 on Malaysia’s preparedness for the haze and the possibility of introducing a transboundary haze pollution law.
Yii said the ministry cited difficulties in obtaining evidence, conducting investigations and enforcing laws against parties outside Malaysia’s jurisdiction.
“These constraints should not be used as an excuse for us not to take firm action,” he said.
He called for the proposed law to be brought before a parliamentary select committee so that MPs could work towards legislation that was effective and enforceable.
Yii also urged Malaysia to raise the issue at the next Asean meeting and push for stronger action under the bloc’s Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.

Khoo said he had submitted a motion to the Dewan Rakyat speaker seeking a debate on the haze, which he described as a national crisis affecting public health, safety, the economy and the wellbeing of Malaysians.
He also said Malaysian companies should face firm action if they were found to be involved in fires in Indonesia.

“Existing laws must be used against them. If there are no applicable laws, the government should issue a stern warning and take other measures, such as blacklisting or boycotting the company, where possible,” he said.

1c9558d381626972: Every piece of AI content from Google's Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic. SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It's going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it's available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.

SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google's trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model's output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple "yes" or "no."

Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google's previous detector was that it only checked for Google's version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn't be flagged in Google's detector. That's no longer a problem.

fc82fe289987d518: SINGAPURA: Singapura akan memasukkan vaksinasi Covid-19 ke dalam Jadual Imunisasi Kanak-Kanak Kebangsaan (NCIS) dan Jadual Imunisasi Dewasa Kebangsaan (NAIS) bermula 12 Okt.

Kementerian Kesihatan dan Agensi Penyakit Berjangkit (CDA) dalam satu kenyataan bersama memaklumkan, vaksinasi Covid-19 telah ditawarkan di bawah Program Vaksinasi Kebangsaan (NVP) sejak 2020 bagi memudah cara pengambilan vaksin semasa wabak.

"Memandangkan Covid-19 akan terus menular dan menimbulkan risiko penyakit teruk, terutamanya dalam kalangan warga emas dan individu berisiko dari segi kesihatan, vaksinasi Covid-19 akan ditambah ke dalam NCIS dan NAIS bagi memastikan vaksin itu kekal mudah diakses dan berpatutan untuk orang ramai," menurut kenyataan itu pada Rabu.
Vaksin berkenaan disyorkan kepada individu berusia 60 tahun ke atas, individu berisiko dari segi kesihatan berusia enam bulan ke atas, dan penghuni kemudahan penjagaan warga emas.
"Selain itu, pekerja kesihatan serta individu yang tinggal atau bekerja bersama individu berisiko dari segi kesihatan digalakkan menerima vaksin bagi membantu melindungi orang di sekeliling mereka.
"Individu lain berumur enam bulan ke atas yang ingin menerima vaksin Covid-19 juga boleh terus berbuat demikian," menurut kenyataan itu.
095815b1fb2713cf: There’s been something of a change in the world of motorsport over the past few years. It has to do with where the money comes from. In the old days, it was tobacco and, to a lesser extent, booze. Today such things are mostly banned, and when you look at a racecar covered in sponsor logos, you’re likely to see something crypto-, cyber-, or AI-related.

This makes sense—an ever-larger share of our GDP is wrapped up in those segments. They’re the ones with all the money, and it takes money to go racing. So at the amateur level, we’ve seen tech CEOs replace dentists as the privateer of choice: This past weekend’s Petit Le Mans included co-founders of GitHub, CrowdStrike, Shopify, and the creator of Ruby on Rails, to name a few.

But this is an instance where a sponsor can provide tangible benefits to their motorsports partner beyond a bank transfer, as Chip Ganassi Racing (CGR) and OpenAI have been showing in IndyCar this year.
78323e4a4dc5db01: PETALING JAYA: Former Klang MP Charles Santiago has urged the government to include initiatives in the 2027 budget to upskill at least 1,000 Indian youths and reduce the school dropout rate in the community.
Santiago said the government should set a specific target of 1,000 Indian youths for upskilling, with candidates identified through schools, open applications, and NGOs.
He said the training could be delivered through technical and vocational education and training (TVET) and other programmes, with particular emphasis on cybersecurity and digital occupations.
He urged the government to develop specific efforts to prevent Indian students from leaving the school system, also focusing on a target number, such as 1,000 students.

He said the high dropout rate, particularly among students who did not pursue further education after SPM, could be addressed by providing them with opportunities to develop skills through TVET and other vocational programmes.
This would give them an alternative pathway to acquire practical, industry-relevant skills, gain qualifications and secure employment.
“Such programmes could also help keep vulnerable youths engaged in education or training and reduce the risk of them being drawn into negative influences, including gang recruitment,” he said.
Santiago also cautioned against framing the issue simply as a problem of “gangsterism” among Indians, saying this could unfairly stigmatise the community.
He said the government should set up a Cabinet committee on Indian affairs chaired by the prime minister.
“The committee would bring together senior ministers and secretaries-general of ministries to directly coordinate and accelerate policies affecting the Indian community,” he said.
Its immediate focus should be expanding skills training and addressing school dropouts.

In August, a coalition of 19 Indian NGOs known as Gelombang Saksama proposed establishing a dedicated statutory body, a public-private funding vehicle and a Cabinet committee to address the Indian community’s socio-economic challenges.

Santiago, who spoke for the coalition, had said the Cabinet committee should be set up as soon as possible to lay the groundwork for establishing the funding vehicle, as well as the dedicated statutory body.
ccccc503e61b42e2: European mobile operators are gaining a slightly larger share of smartphone sales, not because they are selling more devices, but because other sales channels are shrinking faster. This is according to market watcher Counterpoint Research, which says that sales of new smartphones through European operators were down by 4 percent during the second quarter of this year, compared with the same period a year ago. But device sales through the open market fared much worse, declining by 11 percent. This refers to phones that are bought outright from independent retailers or directly from manufacturers, which are typically SIM-free and unlocked so the customer can choose which network they hook up to. Operators accounted for 36 percent of European smartphone sales in the second quarter, up from 35 percent a year earlier. The open market still represented the majority. As The Register has covered numerous times this year, mobile phones have been hit by the AI-driven memory crisis, which has led to a shortage of the DRAM and NAND flash components needed for consumer kit like smartphones and PCs. The resulting rise in prices has been felt most keenly at the lower end of the market, effectively making it commercially unviable to produce budget devices, according to some reports. Phones sold through operators tend to be higher-end models than those bought on the open market. Contracts spread the handset cost over monthly payments, making expensive devices more accessible. Apple played a key part in this slight shift, Counterpoint says, overtaking Samsung as the brand with the greatest market share in Europe's operator channel. Motorola and vivo are highlighted as the fastest-growing bands in the same segment. Counterpoint associate director Jan Stryjak said operators were likely to keep gaining market share for the next few quarters at least, as the lower end of the market continues to be impacted by the memory crisis. "However, we are seeing a steady increase in promotional activity by independent retailers compared to operators, which could mitigate some of the price rises and provide additional stimulus to the open market," he said. Or perhaps more buyers might turn to the second-hand market instead, which has been predicted to see a rise in trade of 12 percent this year, as rising prices make new phones less affordable. Counterpoint forecast that 80 percent of top-flight smartphones will feature agentic AI capabilities by 2027, meaning they will have software agents making decisions and carrying out actions on the owner's behalf. ®
07ff546fa792a2d6: JOHOR BAHRU: Semua sekolah di Johor ditutup dua hari bermula esok susulan keadaan jerebu dan kemerosotan kualiti udara di semua daerah.

Exco Pendidikan dan Penerangan negeri Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali berkata, keputusan berkenaan dibuat atas titah Pemangku Sultan Johor Tunku Mahkota Ismail sebagai langkah berjaga-jaga demi menjaga keselamatan serta kesihatan murid.
Sepanjang tempoh penutupan itu, katanya, sesi Pengajaran dan Pembelajaran di Rumah (PdPR) akan dilaksanakan bagi memastikan proses pembelajaran dapat diteruskan.

Katanya, sekolah yang terlibat dengan pelaksanaan Matriks Pembelajaran Tahun 4 (MPT4) atau mana-mana pentaksiran akan ditangguhkan dan dijadualkan semula tertakluk ketetapan Jabatan Pendidikan Negeri Johor (JPNJ) dan pihak berkaitan.
"Kerajaan negeri memahami bahawa keputusan ini mungkin memberi kesan kepada urusan ibu bapa serta penjaga yang masih perlu bekerja," katanya dalam kenyataan.

"Justeru, kerjasama dan pertimbangan para majikan amat dihargai untuk memberikan fleksibiliti yang bersesuaian kepada ibu bapa yang terkesan, termasuk pengaturan kerja yang munasabah mengikut kesesuaian organisasi masing-masing."
Muhammad Naqib berkata, kerajaan negeri bersama agensi berkaitan akan terus memantau perkembangan bacaan Indeks Pencemaran Udara (IPU) dari semasa ke semasa.
Beliau berkata, keputusan penutupan menuntut sedikit penyesuaian daripada semua pihak, namun keselamatan dan kesihatan anak-anak perlu menjadi keutamaan bersama.
Sehubungan dengan itu, beliau menyeru ibu bapa dan penjaga supaya sentiasa memantau kesihatan anak-anak, mengurangkan aktiviti di luar rumah.
Katanya, ibu bapa juga perlu memastikan pengambilan air secukupnya serta mendapatkan rawatan segera sekiranya mengalami gejala seperti batuk, sakit tekak atau sesak nafas.

Setakat 5 petang tadi, beberapa lokasi di Johor merekodkan bacaan IPU tahap tidak sihat, iaitu Segamat (179), Batu Pahat (177), Pasir Gudang (176), Larkin (172), Tangkak (169) Pengerang (167), Kota Tinggi (166) dan Kluang (165).
0a185023e5a9d7aa: From Ng Sze Fung
Every year, Malaysia’s healthcare debate returns to the same question: how much more should the government spend? The 2027 budget will be no different.
There will be calls for more doctors, more nurses, better hospitals, newer equipment and higher allocations.
All of these are necessary and known. But throwing more money into the same administrative structure will only get us so far.
The harder question is more structural in nature.

Malaysia runs a highly centralised public healthcare system. That model has important strengths. National financing and common standards help prevent access to healthcare from depending entirely on where someone lives.

But centralisation also creates rigidity. The healthcare needs of Selangor, Penang, Kelantan, Sabah and Sarawak are not identical, yet staffing, service planning and resource decisions still operate largely through the same federal machinery.

The answer is not simply to create 13 separate health systems. Nor can healthcare simply be “handed over” to the states. The Federal Constitution is clear. Under the Ninth Schedule, medicine and health fall under the Federal List, while public health, sanitation and disease prevention sit partly within the Concurrent List.
Any serious proposal for decentralisation must therefore work within this constitutional structure, not pretend it does not exist.

Fortunately, decentralisation need not be equated with constitutional disruption. The federal government can continue to finance healthcare, set national standards, regulate professions and medicines, and redistribute resources between richer and poorer states.
At the same time, states or regional health authorities could be given greater discretion over how services are delivered locally.

That could mean more flexibility in workforce deployment, clinic and hospital planning, maintenance spending, primary care integration and partnerships with private providers where public capacity is stretched.
Local authorities could also play a larger role in preventive health, particularly where healthcare overlaps with sanitation, urban design and community wellbeing.

The guiding principle should be simple: centralise what protects equity, decentralise what benefits from local knowledge. The biggest risk is postcode healthcare, where richer states pull ahead while poorer states struggle.
That is why financing should remain largely federal, with allocations based on population need, age, disease burden, geography and deprivation.

Sarawak could provide a useful starting point. The state has already pushed for greater healthcare autonomy under the Malaysia Agreement 1963, including greater control over healthcare planning and the decentralisation of certain regulatory functions to the Sarawak health department, arguments shaped in part by the realities of delivering healthcare across a vast and dispersed population.
Rather than treating Sarawak as an exception, its experience could serve as a practical test of how greater local discretion can operate within a federally financed health system.
Malaysia needs to make its healthcare system less administratively rigid.

If the 2027 budget is serious about reform, the debate should not stop at how much more healthcare receives. It should also ask who is best placed to decide how that money is used, and perhaps the states are the best place to start that discussion in the spirit of decentralisation.
Ng Sze Fung is a senior analyst with Bait Al Amanah, a think tank.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
3400d9fef8a4ddba: KUALA LUMPUR: Kementerian Kesihatan (KKM) mencadangkan agar perlindungan atau caruman insurans kesihatan diwajibkan ke atas pelarian dan pemohon suaka yang berdaftar bagi membantu menampung kos rawatan mereka, sekali gus mengelakkan tunggakan bil perubatan baharu.
Timbalan Menteri Kesihatan Hanifah Hajar Taib memaklumkan Dewan Rakyat, cadangan itu patut terpakai bagi pelarian dan pemohon suaka yang berdaftar di bawah sistem Dokumen Pendaftaran Pelarian (DPP).
Beliau berkata, lebih 80% tunggakan bil perubatan membabitkan pesakit bukan warganegara berpunca daripada pendatang tanpa izin atau individu tanpa kerakyatan.
Bagaimanapun, katanya, kementerian tetap perlu memastikan setiap pesakit diberi rawatan atas dasar kemanusiaan, khususnya bagi kes yang mengancam nyawa.
“Langkah ini selaras dengan Deklarasi Geneva, Sumpah Hippocrates serta Deklarasi Alma-Ata 1978,” katanya ketika menggulung perbahasan Laporan Ketua Audit Negara mengenai kewangan KKM.
Hanifah berkata, jumlah keseluruhan akaun belum terima kementerian menurun daripada RM359 juta pada 2024 kepada RM336 juta pada 2025, iaitu penurunan sebanyak RM23 juta atau 6.4%.
Menurutnya, bil perubatan tidak berbayar membabitkan warga asing bukan semata-mata disebabkan oleh kelemahan dalam kutipan fi rawatan.

Sebaliknya, keadaan itu turut dikaitkan dengan kekangan kewangan pesakit, ketiadaan perlindungan insurans, pesakit yang meninggalkan fasiliti kesihatan tanpa membuat bayaran, serta maklumat pengenalan diri dan butiran perhubungan yang tidak lengkap atau tidak tepat.
“Faktor-faktor ini menyukarkan KKM mengesan pesakit terbabit dan mengambil tindakan susulan bagi tujuan kutipan," katanya.

Beliau berkata, fasiliti kesihatan awam telah mengambil pelbagai langkah untuk mendapatkan semula bayaran berkenaan, termasuk mengeluarkan tiga surat peringatan secara berkala, menghantar tuntutan atau notis perundangan, menghubungi kedutaan atau waris pesakit, menuntut bayaran daripada majikan, serta bekerjasama dengan NGO bagi membantu melunaskan bil pesakit yang tidak mampu membayarnya.

Selain itu, kementerian turut memperkukuh pendekatan 'kutip bayaran sebelum discaj' dengan mewajibkan bayaran deposit dan bayaran ansuran semasa rawatan, memperluas pilihan transaksi tanpa tunai, serta memperhebat pemantauan akaun belum terima.

Hanifah berkata, kerjasama dengan pihak majikan, syarikat insurans dan NGO juga sedang dipergiat, manakala nilai jaminan bank yang dikenakan ke atas majikan serta syarikat swasta akan dinaikkan selaras dengan peningkatan kos rawatan.
205a7d63655f69e5: I found the trailer for Digger intriguing, starring a nearly unrecognizable Tom Cruise and giving off strong Dr. Strangelove vibes. Plus, it is four-time Oscar-winning director Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s (Birdman) first English-language film since 2015’s The Revenant. dfa7d7ca31bbad39: PABNA (Bangladesh), Oct 7 — Bangladesh is preparing to switch on its first nuclear power plant, a long-delayed project promising relief from chronic electricity shortages — even as some fear living beside it.

The 2.4-gigawatt Rooppur nuclear plant, a US$13-billion (RM53.1 billion) project more than a decade in the making, has transformed the once sleepy nearby village of the same name, bringing Russian workers, new businesses and jobs.

Once fully operational, its two reactors are expected to supply more than 10 per cent of electricity demand in the South Asian nation of 170 million people, which has been hit hard by the fuel crisis sparked by the conflict in the Middle East.

For Md Zahedul Hasan, managing director of state-owned Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh, the giant complex represents the culmination of a decades-old ambition to bring nuclear power to the country.

The plant’s first reactor is scheduled to be turned on by the end of this year, and the second unit “will be operational within a year”, Hasan said at the site on the banks of the Padma River, 150 kilometres (93 miles) west of Dhaka.
Bangladesh’s power sector is dominated by fossil fuels, particularly natural gas, with coal, oil and renewables making up the rest.
‘Changed me’
The project, built with Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom, has also brought an unlikely Russian enclave to rural Bangladesh.
Thousands of Russian workers have spent years building and installing equipment, with a residential complex, shops and restaurants springing up around them.
Shop signs appear in Bangla, English and Russian, while some restaurants serve borscht soup alongside local dishes.
Alexander Vladimirovich Skvortsov, a Russian installation technician, said he had a choice between working in Turkey or Bangladesh. He chose Rooppur, moving there with his family in 2024.
“When I first saw the construction site at Rooppur, I realized how much work lay ahead on this project... honestly, Rooppur changed me and my life,” he told AFP.
The project has also transformed the local economy.
Md Emon Khan, 28, left his garment-factory job in Dhaka and returned to Rooppur, where he now sells vegetables and fruit to workers.
“I can speak a bit of Russian, and they can speak Bangla, too,” he said.
Plant officials say stringent safety measures have been followed and lessons from previous nuclear accidents were incorporated into the project.
Standing near a radiation monitoring tower and an alarm post, 15-year-old Mohammad Nafiz said he saw little to fear.
“We are glad that Rooppur is known to the world, and my friends and I hope that we will work at the plant after graduating from engineering schools,” he added.
Not everyone shares that confidence.
Md Yunus Ali, 80, whose home is a 15-minute walk from the plant, said opposition to building a nuclear facility in the densely populated area dates back decades.
“A few days ago, they ran a compressor test with a big bang... even the children who were asleep woke up in fear,” said Ali, a retired paper mill worker.
“I am old now, and I am not afraid for my life... but I have children and grandchildren, and I want safety for them.”
‘Full benefit’
The ambition to build a nuclear power plant at Rooppur dates back to the 1960s.
Several attempts came after independence, including approaches to Saudi Arabia and France, and talks with China and South Korea. No deals materialised.
Bangladesh finally signed an agreement with Moscow in 2015, with the Russian state offering a loan covering about 90 per cent of the project’s original cost.
Construction began in 2017.
The project has since faced delays, including disruption from the Covid-19 pandemic and sanctions on Russia after its invasion of Ukraine, which complicated equipment deliveries and payments.
There have also been corruption allegations surrounding the project, including against ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina and members of her family. They have rejected the accusations.
For most Bangladeshis, however, the biggest question is when Rooppur will finally deliver reliable electricity.
Belly Begum, a 55-year-old farmer, struggles to irrigate her land during frequent power cuts.
“I wish the Rooppur nuclear power plant goes into operation soon, and we reap the full benefit,” she said.
“I hope we will get electricity for 24 hours without interruption, as the plant is near my house.” — AFP
2e55e2dc72b86cc4: OSLO, Oct 7 — Donald Trump’s chances of winning the Nobel Peace Prize are seen as minimal, but his “spectre” will cast its shadow over Friday’s announcement of the winner in Oslo, experts say.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee knows it will be under close scrutiny: since his return to the White House in January 2025, the billionaire Republican has campaigned intensively for the prize and hasn’t hidden his disappointment at not winning it yet.

The chances of him getting the nod are however undermined by his war against Iran, his territorial ambitions — sometimes at the expense of allies, as in Greenland — and his attacks on international cooperation institutions and the media.

Even though he has not been lobbying as openly for the Nobel in recent weeks, Trump remains on everyone’s minds, with strong chances that the committee’s pick will, regardless of who they choose, be interpreted as direct or indirect criticism of the US president.
Trump is “the spectre in the room”, said the head of the Peace Research Institute in Oslo (PRIO), Haakon Gjerlow.
He said the Nobel committee must be asking itself: “Is there any potential for this prize to create harm rather than good in awarding it?”, given the reactions that could emerge from the White House.
The Nobel Institute says it is unfazed.

“There’s always a lot of lobbying, and ultimately perhaps also attempts to exert pressure on the committee. So in one sense we’re very used to that,” the secretary of the committee, Kristian Berg Harpviken, told AFP.
“It’s not something we don’t discuss. Of course we have to discuss it, but it’s not like that influences the discussions in the room and decisions that come out,” he insisted.
‘Age of predators’
Last year, the prestigious prize went to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, a choice generally considered palatable to Trump.
Machado even gave him her Nobel gold medal, judging he deserved it after the capture of President Nicolas Maduro — though she failed to obtain his political backing in exchange.
Those events could prompt the committee to this year choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, such as an individual or organisation working to protect children or humanitarian efforts.

That could include the Save the Children charity and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of kids illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories — a cause close to the heart of Trump’s wife Melania.
Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, could also be a potential laureate.
But the committee may also choose a laureate that could rub Trump the wrong way.

That could include the UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese, Pope Leo XIV, press freedoms with an award to the Committee to Protect Journalists, or international justice bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
“We live in an age of predators. We have Trump, Putin, Netanyahu,” said Nobel historian Asle Sveen.
“They don’t want to have an international order. They want to have big powers with spheres of influence. And this court stands in the way,” he said, referring to the ICC.
A total of 287 individuals and organisations have been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize, though the names on the list are kept secret for 50 years.
But peace remains elusive in many parts of the world: 65 armed conflicts involving at least one state actor were registered in 2025, the highest number since 1946, according to PRIO.
“At an overall level, it is clear that the world is not developing in the right direction,” said Harpviken.
“At the same time... there is no lack of good initiatives. There is no lack of organisations or individuals who do good work,” he said.
“A peace prize may make more sense than ever.” — AFP
0b6e591d564929d8: WARSAW, Oct 7 — Assassinated Russian reporter Anna Politkovskaya, shot dead outside her Moscow home in 2006, had “predicted” Russia’s trajectory under Vladimir Putin, her editor told AFP ahead of the 20th anniversary of her death.
Politkovskaya had reported fearlessly on the war in Chechnya and the rise of Putin, warning of his authoritarian tendencies at a time when he was being welcomed and courted in the West.
She was gunned down in the lift of her central Moscow apartment block on October 7, 2006 — Putin’s 54th birthday.
Her killing marked a turning point for Russian journalism.

Two decades on, Putin is still in power, Moscow’s war against Ukraine — which has killed hundreds of thousands — is in its fifth year, and domestic repression has reached levels not seen since the Soviet era.

“Everything that is happening with Russia was predicted by Anna Politkovskaya in the books she published before her death,” Sergei Sokolov, the legendary reporter’s editor at the Novaya Gazeta newspaper where she worked, said.
Moscow has labelled her paper, Novaya Gazeta, a “foreign agent”.
“At the time, nobody believed her and they said she was exaggerating the dangers and fears,” Sokolov said.

As the West embraced Putin in the early 2000s — a strongman leader cautiously welcomed after the chaos of the previous decade — Politkovskaya warned Russian journalists would have to show “total servility to Putin” or face death or prison.
Russia, she said, was “hurling back into a Soviet abyss.”
The gunmen behind her murder are in prison — but the person, or people, who ordered the killing have never been named.
Asked about that in 2021, Putin said his agencies “did everything to uncover these crimes”.

Journalist Sergei Sokolov attends a gathering in memory of the slain Russian reporter Anna Politkovskaya at the office of the Novaya Gazeta newspaper, recently designated by authorities as a ‘foreign agent’, in Moscow October 6, 2026. — AFP pic
‘Nothing could make her stray’
In death, Politkovskaya has become an even more totemic figure for Russian journalists — inspiring a generation of investigative reporters who she never met, and who are now forced to work in exile.
With Russia at war in Ukraine, her reporting from both sides of the frontline in the Chechen wars has taken on fresh relevance.
She covered war crimes committed by both the Russian army and Chechen rebels and pushed both to evacuate civilians.
In 2002, she walked into a Moscow theatre that had been seized by Chechen rebels to try to secure the release of hostages.
“The terrorists had chosen me as a person they wanted to talk to, I couldn’t refuse,” she later said.
More than 130 hostages would be killed when special forces gassed the theatre and stormed the building.
“What stood out in her was her tenacity — nothing could make her stray from the topic or idea she had,” Sokolov, her editor, recalled.
That school of journalism now lies in virtual tatters.
Years of pressure from the Kremlin has culminated in censorship levels unseen since the Soviet Union.
If Politkovskaya were alive, Sokolov was certain: “she would definitely not be able to stay silent”.
In her later years, Politkovskaya had become a fierce critic of Ramzan Kadyrov, then being groomed as the future head of Chechnya.
She dubbed him a “little dragon” and accused him of being given a free hand to brutally rule over the war-torn region in exchange for loyalty to the Kremlin.
Kadyrov in turn called her an “enemy of the Chechen people”, vowing she would “answer” for her criticism of him.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Dmitry Muratov (left), a Nobel Prize-winner, one of the founders of the Novaya Gazeta daily, and journalist Sergei Sokolov (centre) attend a gathering in memory of the slain Russian reporter Anna Politkovskaya at the office of the Novaya Gazeta newspaper, recently designated by authorities as a ‘foreign agent’, in Moscow October 6, 2026. — AFP pic
Icon

Despite her name being virtually erased in Russia’s official narrative, Politkovskaya remains an icon for independent Russian journalists — but also a constant reminder of the dangers of her profession.

“You need an example. If there was no example of courageous journalists and if everyone kept their heads down, then things will be even worse for Russian journalism,” 28-year-old exiled reporter Yegor Feoktistov said.
“Her fate always reminds you of what can happen — but it also gives you courage.”
Another investigative journalist forced to work in exile, Olga Churakova, said she is “surprised by the stream of people who want to become journalists” in Russia despite the dangers.
Many mention Politkovskaya as their inspiration.
“People still come and say: ‘Someone needs to do this job’.” — AFP
344a8e5911cbabd5: ISTANBUL, Oct 7 — Three years into Israel’s genocide in the Gaza Strip, Palestinian and UN data show sweeping consequences for women and girls, from deaths, injuries and disappearances to rising miscarriage rates, unsafe births and malnutrition, Anadolu Ajansi reported.

The collapse of Gaza’s health system has also deprived pregnant women of medical care, forcing some to give birth at home or in displacement shelters, while changes in family structures have left tens of thousands of women responsible for supporting their households.
Data released by the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics on July 18, 2026, showed that 12,400 women, excluding girls, had been killed in Gaza since October 7, 2023.

The bureau also said women and children accounted for 4,700 of the 11,200 people reported missing, with the fate of many still unknown amid fears that some remain under the rubble of destroyed buildings.

UN Women, in an April 2026 report titled The Cost of War on Women and Girls, estimated that more than 38,000 women and girls were killed between October 2023 and December 2025 — an average of nearly 47 per day.
The report added, “there are close to 11,000 women and girls with lifelong injury.”
Survivors continue to face daily risks from bombardment, hunger, repeated displacement and restrictions on access to essential services, the report said.
According to the report, more than 71,200 Palestinians were killed during the period it covered, with women, children and older persons together representing more than half of all fatalities.
It cautioned that the figure was likely lower than the actual death toll “given the collapse of health information and reporting systems.”
The highest proportion of deaths among women and children was recorded during the first six months of the war, when they accounted for nearly two-thirds of documented fatalities.

The report said that despite a ceasefire agreement that took effect on October 10, 2025, women and girls continued to be killed and injured, while humanitarian and health conditions threatening their lives showed no significant improvement.

From the early months of the genocide, rights and health organisations documented a sharp deterioration in women’s reproductive health amid attacks on medical facilities, lack of access to health care, repeated displacement and malnutrition.
In July 2024, the International Planned Parenthood Federation said miscarriages in Gaza had risen by at least 300 per cent during the first nine months of the war.
Physicians for Human Rights said in January 2026 that its report, Destroying Hope for the Future: Reproductive Violence in Gaza, documented 2,600 miscarriages during the first half of 2025.
The report also documented 220 pregnancy-related deaths and 1,460 premature births, while more than 2,500 newborns required intensive care.
Earlier data from Gaza’s Health Ministry showed that 57.1 per cent of registered pregnant women in 2025 suffered from anemia.

Even after the ceasefire, around 15 births per week continued to take place outside hospitals, often without skilled midwives and in unsafe conditions.
Hunger and malnutrition also heightened risks for pregnant women and newborns, including low birth weight, premature delivery, stillbirths and maternal deaths.

The war has also reshaped thousands of families in Gaza, forcing more women to assume responsibility for supporting their households following the deaths, injuries or disappearance of their husbands and the loss of income.

d0e58cec865dbaa0: The Netherlands Tax and Customs Administration has abandoned its planned Microsoft 365 cloud migration in favor of services hosted on infrastructure it controls, alongside European open source alternatives. Email and calendars will move on-premises in 2027, followed by storage and collaboration services later that year and in 2028. The letter to parliament from Eelco Eerenberg, State Secretary for Finance, follows an earlier decision to pause the Microsoft 365 rollout. The tax authority selected Microsoft 365 in 2025, but the decision attracted criticism. In June, the Dutch Advisory Council on ICT Assessment recommended rolling back the cloud services rollout, which had reached about 5,000 of the 47,500 employees across the tax, customs, and benefits services, rather than completing it as planned by the end of 2026. According to the board, the design of Microsoft 365 in the public cloud "falls short on information security, information processing and future-proofing." On security, the board noted concerns about sending confidential documents, which currently travel over government networks, via American servers. The board also criticized reliance on standard Microsoft encryption for sensitive data rather than Double Key Encryption, which would give the administration greater control. End-to-end encryption was not enabled by default for one-to-one Teams calls and was unavailable for group calls under the chosen configuration. To be fair to Microsoft, many of these concerns (for example, around encryption) stem from the design selected. However, others are harder to dismiss. On future-proofing, other concerns included vendor lock-in and the risk of reduced flexibility and sovereignty from choosing a single-supplier solution with one American (cloud) provider. There was also a concern about a lack of an exit strategy for when the Tax and Customs Administration wanted to move on to more sovereign alternatives. In this week's letter, Eerenberg wrote: "In 2027, the provision for mail and calendar will be realized on-premises. Later in 2027 and 2028, European open source solutions for personal storage and collaboration functionalities will follow. This allows us to work toward a sustainable and more autonomous solution for these functionalities." Increased datacenter capacity has made the on-premises option possible, Eerenberg said. The revised approach will reuse existing licenses where possible to limit additional investment. The reversal creates complications for records management, however. Some planned capabilities in the Microsoft 365 package are unavailable on-premises, and the administration is still assessing how to replace them. Microsoft is no stranger to public bodies in the Netherlands, and a recent report showed that a majority used the company's cloud services. However, concerns about US authorities' ability to compel disclosure of data held by US providers under the CLOUD Act have loomed large in recent years. The risk has prompted European governments to consider reducing their dependence on US providers and moving to more sovereign solutions. It is early days, and agencies report teething trouble switching. A colorful report from Politico quoted an unnamed European Commission staffer describing the Teams alternative supplied by Element as "absolute shit" on an internal message board. The report does not establish how widespread those complaints are. The Matrix protocol underpinning Element's software also powers the French public sector messaging service, Tchap. Element boss Matthew Hodgson was upbeat about the European Commission deployment, telling The Register: "We've only had positive and constructive feedback from our actual customers; the leaders and IT functions that are driving sovereignty. "There's inevitably a few unhappy change-resistant users in large deployments, but we work in lockstep with our customers to gather feedback and incorporate it, especially during the trial phase." As for sovereignty more widely in Europe, Hodgson said: "European governments are moving to alternatives that give them greater sovereignty. They can't leave themselves exposed to being deplatformed, and they recognise that traditional centralised technology isn't resilient enough for an increasingly unpredictable geopolitical climate." Frank Karlitschek, founder and CEO of Nextcloud, a vendor of storage and collaboration software, said: "It is great to see Dutch tax authorities have decided to work toward a sovereign digital workplace. This will benefit the resilience of their operations. "European Public sector organizations mostly use software from a few large, proprietary providers, which has led to strong dependencies. "Organizations have recognized the risks of digital dependencies and are looking for better options to have full control over their data, infrastructure, and underlying technology. The organizations now aim to build a more resilient IT stack." Karlitschek noted a trend forming across Europe. According to Nextcloud, it added more than two million sovereign workspace seats in 2025. Microsoft declined to comment. ®

6702fea53e1b1289: IPOH, Oct 7 — The Wildlife and National Parks Department (Perhilitan) will only capture or translocate Malayan tigers if an assessment finds that their presence poses a threat to public safety.

Perak Perhilitan director Dr Pazil Abdul Patah said the assessment takes into account the tiger’s behaviour, frequency and duration of sightings, distance from residential areas, movement patterns, and evidence of interactions or attacks involving humans or livestock.
“If the assessment shows a clear and continuing threat to human safety, Perhilitan will take appropriate action based on technical assessments in the field,” he told Bernama.

Five tiger sightings or incidents have been recorded in Perak from January to October this year, beginning with a report of a roar in Proton City, Tanjung Malim on January 10, followed by an image captured in Bukit Bangkong, Chemor on July 14 and the capture of a tigress in Hulu Kinta on July 22.
This was followed by a fatal attack in Pos Perwor, Sungai Siput on September 21 and the discovery of tiger footprints at Kem Sultan Nazrin Shah, 69 Komando, Ulu Kinta on September 29.

Pazil said tiger sightings near human settlements did not necessarily mean that their forest habitat or roaming areas were shrinking, as movements could also be influenced by prey availability, habitat conditions, human disturbance, development and land use, as well as the animals’ natural movements.
“In some situations, tigers may move through forest edges or ecological corridors within their home range and be detected near human settlements by chance,” he said.

He said Perhilitan continuously monitored prey species such as barking deer, deer and wild boar in the state’s main forest reserves, with camera traps, field surveys and population data used to assess prey availability.

Pazil said complaints about tiger sightings were assessed based on the location, time, physical evidence and current situation to determine the priority and appropriate deployment of personnel, with control teams sent to the field when there was a risk to public safety.

He said besides physical measures such as setting traps, Perhilitan also provided technical advice and safety guidance, including advising residents in high-risk areas to avoid going out alone in the early morning or late evening, refrain from provoking tigers and leave the handling of such cases to the department. — Bernama

2205e07f2ba18dce: STOCKHOLM, Oct 7 — France’s Henri Kagan and Japan’s Kenso Soai today won the Nobel chemistry prize for solving the mystery of why only one version of some molecules’ mirror-image forms appears in nature, a discovery decisive for the development of pharmaceuticals.
The pair were honoured “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”, the jury said.
Like hands, all amino acids exist as two mirrored variants, but only one of them is found in the proteins in the body’s cells.
The other is rarely found in nature, a phenomenon known as “homochirality”, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained.
Chemists have long wondered how that process occurs, and the two Nobel laureates’ discoveries have “enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality”, the jury said.

“Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular,” said Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry.
“Their discoveries have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals,” the jury said.
Last year, the chemistry prize went to Japan’s Susumu Kitagawa, UK-born Richard Robson and American-Jordanian Omar Yaghi for developing a method of designing molecular structures.

The chemistry prize follows the physics prize, which yesterday honoured Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for groundbreaking work using Antarctic ice to capture particles originating in the distant cosmos.
On Monday, the medicine prize was awarded to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel.

The literature laureate will be revealed tomorrow, with some pundits suggesting that the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a prize for a woman writer, possibly from Latin America.
The most keenly anticipated award — the peace prize — is due on Friday.
US President Donald Trump lobbied intensively last year to get the prize and the committee is aware he will be watching closely again.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
The Nobel consists of a diploma, a gold medal and a 12-million-kronor (RM4.9-million) prize sum, which is shared if there is more than one winner in a discipline.
The laureates will receive their prizes at a formal ceremony on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of scientist Alfred Nobel, who created the prizes in his will. — AFP

f356471a4a624ca9: The FBI and US Secret Service (USSS) say criminals using credentials linked to the FortiBleed campaign are locking organizations out of their Fortinet firewalls. The agencies published a joint advisory on Tuesday, citing SOCRadar's verification of more than 86,644 compromised devices across 194 countries. "Based on initial responses, some victims may get locked out of their Fortinet devices if the threat actor either deletes or changes the password for original accounts on the system," their advisory [PDF] states. "During the initial intrusion, threat actors create new accounts not previously on the device. In certain cases, threat actors delete existing accounts to block organizations from accessing affected devices and to maintain persistence on the system while attempting lateral movement within the environment." The campaign targets internet-facing FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways. Criminals use credentials from earlier breaches and infostealer logs for credential stuffing and password spraying, then extract password hashes from compromised devices and crack them offline using GPU-accelerated clusters. The agencies urged organizations to restrict internet-facing management access, terminate active administrative and VPN sessions, reset passwords, and enable phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication. The advisory also links FortiBleed to ransomware campaigns, saying initial access brokers supplied compromised-network access to ransomware affiliates. The Register previously reported on the connection, identified by SOCRadar. The current evidence points to affiliates working for the INC/Lynx and Payload ransomware groups making use of the credentials, and SOCRadar said in July that it had seen at least 12 confirmed ransomware attacks stemming from FortiBleed. The agencies encouraged victims to report incidents, while noting that organizations were not obliged to provide information in response to this advisory. The FBI and the Secret Service said victim reports could help identify indicators of compromise and warned against paying ransoms. ®
93673b3d422ed95c: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 7 — The Malaysian Parliament’s Palestine Caucus will submit a proposed motion on the genocide in Gaza to the Office of the Dewan Rakyat Speaker and seek to have it scheduled for debate during next week’s parliamentary sitting.
Its chairman Syed Ibrahim Syed Noh said the proposed motion would include calls for a lasting ceasefire, the protection of civilians, and safe, sustained and unhindered access to humanitarian aid.

Syed Ibrahim, who is also Deputy Minister of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability, said this at a press conference held in conjunction with the Three-Year Commemoration of the Gaza Genocide at the Parliament building here today.

“In addition, to establish a coordinated Malaysian framework for the recovery of Gaza, prioritising healthcare, education, child rehabilitation and Palestinian-led reconstruction,” he said.

2513f5dbc7a8b2c9: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 7 — The Ministry of Education (MOE) has instructed state education departments (JPN), district education offices (PPD) and all educational institutions under its jurisdiction to continue monitoring the current haze situation in their respective locations to determine further action.

It said educational institutions in the Batu Pahat district, under the supervision of the Johor JPN, are temporarily closed starting today until conditions are safe and further instructions are issued.
According to the Department of Environment’s (DOE) Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) portal, Batu Pahat recorded an API reading of 190 as of 10 am today.
Following the closure, home-based teaching and learning (PdPR) will be implemented based on suitability and current directives, taking into account the students’ safety, health and well-being.
“Based on the current haze situation and the latest API readings recorded nationwide, the Johor JPN has taken follow-up measures in accordance with the guidelines established by the MOE,” it added.

“The JPN, PPD and all educational institutions under the MOE must also remain vigilant and monitor API readings and the latest status via the DOE’s website at https://eqms.doe.gov.my/APIMS/main on a regular basis to safeguard the health of students and the education community,” it added.
