ce54eafcfc8a3510: The problem with the Sports Development (Amendment) Bill 2026 is not simply how much power it gives the youth and sports minister.
It is where that power stops.
The Dewan Rakyat passed the Bill on Tuesday after 31 MPs debated it, amid concerns that the proposed Section 41A could give the minister sweeping authority over sports bodies.

Under the provision, the minister may declare a sports body unlawful if it is used for purposes harmful to national security, public order or morality. The order would cancel its registration after consultation with the sports commissioner.

Minister Dr Taufiq Johari has stressed that this is not a blank cheque. He said disagreement with the government, internal disputes or unhappiness with a sports body’s leadership would not, by themselves, justify action.
He also said the provision would rely on existing laws and offences and remain open to judicial review.
Those safeguards matter but they do not remove the central question.
If the sports commissioner is supposed to be the regulator, why is the most drastic regulatory power being placed in the hands of the politician who appoints the regulator?
That is the issue Parliament should continue examining before the Bill becomes law.
A stronger commissioner, but a stronger minister too
The Bill does not merely increase ministerial power. It also strengthens the sports commissioner.

Registered sports bodies will need the commissioner’s approval before changing their name, address or constitution, while the commissioner can direct amendments to bring a constitution into line with the law. The Bill also creates a stronger enforcement and investigation framework.
That creates an awkward structure. The commissioner becomes a stronger regulator while the minister retains the power to take the most serious action against a sports body.
There are therefore two centres of authority without a clearly independent layer between them.
That raises a basic question: who regulates Malaysian sport — the political ministry or an independent sporting regulator?
The answer should not depend on the personality of whoever happens to hold the minister’s post.

The sports commissioner is appointed by the minister, while the office already has substantial regulatory powers under the Sports Development Act 1997, including registration and deregistration functions.
The new Bill adds to those responsibilities rather than creating a fundamentally separate regulator.

If Malaysia genuinely wants a strong sports commissioner, perhaps the next step should be to make the office more institutionally independent from the minister, not merely more powerful under the minister.
That could mean clearer safeguards around appointments, tenure, removal and appeals. The precise model is open to debate.
The principle is harder to dispute: strong institutions also need strong boundaries between them.

The government has said it wants better governance and accountability in sport. The test is whether the new structure makes those institutions stronger, rather than simply making the executive stronger.
Deregistration is not a minor penalty
Section 41A deserves particular scrutiny because deregistration can go far beyond stopping an association from operating.

Under the Bill, assets of a deregistered sports body can vest in the director-general of insolvency for the winding-up of its affairs and settlement of debts. A new body may seek to take over its assets and liabilities with High Court approval.
Deregistration is therefore not simply a warning or suspension. It can end a sports body’s legal existence, trigger the winding-up of its affairs and disrupt control of its assets and liabilities.
Such a power may be necessary in extreme cases. A sports body used to finance terrorism, organise violence or facilitate serious criminal activity cannot expect registration to provide protection.
The minister has cited terrorism, subversive or espionage activity, riots and violence, and serious forms of sexual exploitation and trafficking as examples of the intended threshold.
But Parliament should still ask whether those limits belong clearly enough in the law itself.

The word “morality”, in particular, can carry a wide meaning. What evidence must be produced? Who decides when the threshold has been crossed? Must the conduct involve an offence under existing law? Does the sports body get a meaningful opportunity to answer the allegations before its registration disappears?
Those questions are not obstacles to enforcement. They are safeguards against arbitrary enforcement.
If the government’s position is that Section 41A will apply only in serious circumstances already covered by law, spelling that out more tightly would strengthen the provision.
The football citizenship scandal inevitably surfaced during the debate, with MPs warning against concentrating too much authority in one political office.
But this should not become a FAM story. The more useful question is: what lessons from FAM should be written into the institutional architecture of Malaysian sport?
If the episode exposed weaknesses in governance, accountability, documentation or decision-making, the answer cannot simply be to give the government more power over sports bodies.
It should be to make the system harder to circumvent, with clearer duties, better records, transparent procedures and credible independent review.
Malaysia already has rules, registration requirements and enforcement powers. Yet 4,687 sports associations and clubs were recorded as inactive or problematic between 2020 and 2025.
The figure included 23 national bodies, 206 state bodies, 486 district bodies and 3,972 clubs, with some found to have breached their constitutions or the Sports Development Act.
The issue, then, is not simply whether the law has enough teeth. It is whether the system can make sports bodies comply and govern themselves properly.
The commissioner already has considerable authority. The bigger challenge is making the regulatory system work consistently and effectively.
That is why strengthening the office should mean more than adding powers. It should mean bolstering its independence and accountability too.

The government has also stressed the need for better governance and accountability in sport. The new legislation therefore needs to draw a clear line between legitimate public regulation and political control of sport.
The Bill has passed the Dewan Rakyat, but it is not yet law. It still has to go through the Dewan Negara before royal assent and gazettal. That leaves room to tighten the framework.
The question is not whether the state should act against a sports body that genuinely threatens national security or public order. It should.
The question is who decides when that threshold has been crossed, on what evidence, under what process and with what independent scrutiny.
The amendment strengthens both ends of the regulatory chain. The minister gets a formidable new power. The sports commissioner gets stronger regulatory powers.
What it does not yet appear to provide is a sufficiently independent middle or appellate layer.
The problem is not power. It is where the power stops.

33e7c0fc3e390095: Last month at Rails World 2026, Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson gave a relentlessly optimistic keynote in which he suggested AI has all but eliminated the need for developers to manually write code. But perhaps DHH, as he is known online, shouldn’t delete his code editor quite yet. On Sunday, DHH posted about a test in which he had frontier agents implement and optimize his company’s Campfire group chat app in three languages: Elixir, Go, and Rust. He then compared the runtime performance of those versions with the original Ruby on Rails implementation. DHH’s post includes data that seemingly demonstrates the efficiency of the Rust programming language, and AI agent coding itself. But many observers came to another conclusion: Don't trust DHH’s benchmarks. As of press time, the post and accompanying chart garnered over 900,000 views. It showed the Rust rewrite of the chat app outperformed others by a wide margin on five tasks, including searching or posting a message. DHH did not say which AI services he used for these rewrites, but noted that each rewrite took only a few hours, as the original code itself, largely written in Ruby, is relatively compact. Many observers, notably advocates of other languages, quickly surmised from the source material that DHH had optimized the Rust results but didn't do the same for the other languages he tested. Whither high-level languages? Rewriting applications in Rust, often with the help of AI agents, seems to be a popular undertaking these days, with Microsoft's Copilot runtime, the pnpm JavaScript installer, and the Bun JavaScript toolchain all getting the Rust treatment. In DHH’s test, the Rust implementation handily bested the others across all five workloads, sometimes by a wide margin. To serve a “room page,” for instance, Rust knocked out 36,260 requests per second. In contrast, Ruby on Rails was only able to fulfill a paltry 241 requests, while Elixir delivered 722 requests, and even runner-up Golang only knocked out 3,860 requests a second. Rust executed the other tasks with similar alacrity, easily besting the other languages DHH used. The takeaway was obvious to DHH: Rewriting an application in Rust, or better yet having AI agents do the job, may very well result in major performance improvements for an app. DHH suggested that many factors go into choosing a programming language for a particular job, and execution speed is not the sole criterion. Rust can be agonizingly slow to compile, and for many, writing or even reading Rust code is an arduous job. DHH himself began developing Rails in 2003 while building Basecamp in the then relatively obscure Ruby programming language to ease the developer experience. He doesn’t seem to mind that Ruby ranked the slowest in his own tests. “I didn't care about [performance] when the pay-off was huge in terms of productivity and developer joy.” But AI agents don’t give a hoot about joy. “You really have to bury your head in the sand not to see that when agents write the code and validate the output, we need to adjust to a new reality,” he wrote. Chips on the table DHH’s ad-hoc test was quickly met with skepticism, criticism and outright mockery, especially on X. (It’s as if DHH’s conservative views on immigration and his work to bring yet another Linux desktop into the world didn’t give him enough headaches). “What worries me about the future of programming is you see this and don’t immediately know there must be something wrong with the results or what you actually measured,” wrote prominent Google engineer Jaana Dogan in an X response to DHH’s tests. Dogan did not elaborate on the test’s shortcomings, but many others, especially advocates of other languages, were more than happy to provide details. One Elixir advocate called DHH’s implementation “moronic,” while a couple of others actually rewrote the Elixir code to make its performance comparable to Rust’s. After that rewrite, the Elixir version of the app bested Rust’s performance on some tasks, despite further third-party Rust optimizations. DHH expressed surprise that others would assume a high-level language like Elixir or Ruby could even compete with a language like Rust, which runs closer to the metal. But he also noted on X that “It's not exactly extra points for Elixir if frontier agents can't find the magic ‘go fast’ switches.” Elsewhere, observers noted that the Rust rewrite got a lot more post-coding attention than the other implementations of Go and Elixir, both of which seemed to be quickly wrapped up after the initial agent requests. “You're not benchmarking languages, you're benchmarking how much attention each port got,” one observer wrote on X. Golang advocates were likewise unamused. “The benchmark was unfair. More time was put into the Rust code while the rest were one-shotted,” one wrote on X. Someone else even made their own chart showing how much more the Rust code was tuned compared to the quick passes on the other languages. None of these rebuttals actually negates DHH’s advocacy of using agents to code. But clearly, skipping a manual review of the resulting work will still leave a lot of potential gains on the table. ®
056560778e3ea72a: System76 is banning AI-generated content from contributions to the COSMIC desktop. Some GNOME sub-projects also restrict AI-generated contributions, but one developer is urging them to make an exception for vulnerability reports. The COSMIC desktop project has changed its contributors' guidelines. The latest version now has a clear no-AI rule, insisting that contributors declare: "I have not included any LLM (also known as AI) generated content in this PR, including code, comments, and descriptions." In other words, you can teach yourself using AI, you can find bugs with AI, but if you want to submit your code for inclusion in COSMIC, you can't use AI to write the code, its docs or notes, or even the submission requests. This position is in keeping with some other desktop projects. For instance, the GNOME Calendar guide to contributing says: "This project does not allow contributions generated by large languages [sic] models (LLMs) and chatbots." GNOME Extensions also restricts AI-generated submissions, although it permits AI learning aids and code completion. Its review guidelines spell it out: "Extensions must not be AI-generated." COSMIC is one of the newest complete Linux desktop environments, but even so, it's been under development for years. The Register first reported on the effort nearly five years ago, meaning that it's older than ChatGPT, which debuted in late 2022 (it only feels so very much longer). COSMIC does use some GNOME components, and its default config looks not unlike GNOME, with a top panel and a dock-like launcher at the bottom. There are good reasons for that: the original System76 desktop called "COSMIC" was based on GNOME, quite heavily customized with GNOME extensions. Saying that, though, this new COSMIC is a very different beast. Its first stable release shipped with Pop!_OS 24.04 in late 2025. Although it looks similar, it's an entirely new, ground-up effort, written in Rust using the Iced toolkit. COSMIC itself is Wayland-only. GNOME is much older, larger, and more complicated. The project was announced in 1997, the year after the KDE project announcement. KDE 1.0 came out in 1998, and GNOME 1.0 in 1999. In part, GNOME was a response to KDE. KDE is built on the Qt toolkit, which was not fully open source. As such, in KDE's early days, Red Hat refused to include it in Red Hat Linux. Qt is aimed at C++ developers, so KDE was built in C++. Linux, like Unix, is built in plain old C and many Unix traditionalists scorned the much more complex C++. So GNOME was built in plain old C, using GTK, the toolkit built for the GIMP. In 1998, Red Hat Linux 5.1 included a preview of GNOME, and by Red Hat Linux 6.0 in 1999, GNOME 1.0 was the default desktop. GNOME is still the default desktop in RHEL to this day, and many GNOME developers' day jobs are at Red Hat. As we noted back in March, Red Hat management is noticeably enthusiastic about AI – although six months later, it was capping developers' AI spend. GNOME is largely written in C, which lacks automatic memory safety guarantees, although other languages feature too: GNOME Shell combines JavaScript and C, and some components are written in the GNOME-centric Vala programming language. Michael Catanzaro, GNOME developer, just published a blog post titled "The Era of Software Quality, or the Era of Ostriches?" which argues that the GNOME project must accept AI-generated bug reports. This is not a new subject for him. His post links to an earlier one from June, "Please Do Not Ban AI-Assisted Issue Reports." The following month, he announced a reduction in the disclosure deadline for issues reported to GNOME Security, from 90 days to 30, effective August 1. We recently reported on the 1,313 CVE identifiers listed in Debian's latest Linux kernel security advisory. AI is resulting in the discovery of vast numbers of bugs in the equally vast codebases of modern FOSS. GNOME is one of the biggest desktops in the Linux and BSD world, with much of its code written in memory-unsafe languages. As Catanzaro says: "No matter how much we try, GNOME developers will fail [to] write secure code when using unsafe languages like C, C++, or Vala: it's just too hard for even experienced developers to do properly." We are not arguing that Catanzaro is wrong. Given the stance toward AI of GNOME's biggest sponsor, it is entirely in keeping, and he makes a strong case. All we are noting is that this could in time prove to be the thin edge of a wedge with the weight of Red Hat behind it. First the project allows AI-generated bug reports. From there, it would not be a huge step to allowing AI-assisted triage. From there, to AI-assisted fixes. Once you're letting AI-assisted code in, then AI-assisted extensions may not seem so extreme, then core components, and in time, to the desktop itself. It would be wildly controversial, just as it already is in the KDE project. That doesn't mean it won't happen – in either project. Debian decided to allow it, and of course, the kernel itself does too. ®
7122d0367cc70c69: The role of meeting rooms is changing. Traditionally, they were formal spaces built around a large central table and inflexible physical setup, reserved primarily for board meetings, client presentations, or official status updates. The rise of hybrid work and advances in collaboration technology have made that approach increasingly obsolete. Employees now come into the office to connect, collaborate, and brainstorm with colleagues rather than to undertake the solo, focused work they can do better at home. The upshot is that many meeting rooms have transformed into fluid, digitized, data-enabled hubs. With modular partitions, movable furniture, and casual seating, they are designed to adapt to whatever task is at hand. As digital nodes, they also bridge the gap between remote and office workers, so remote and in-person participants get a consistent experience regardless of location. That shift is only possible because of the convergence between IT and audio-visual (AV) equipment, explains Yannic Laleeuwe, marketing director for Barco's ClickShare visualization, collaboration, and networking platform. Cameras, microphones, and wireless conferencing, collaboration and presentation tools, such as ClickShare can now connect to enterprise networks. That allows management through centralized cloud-based systems, so IT teams can monitor, update, secure and tune these systems in ways they could not before. "Historically, meeting rooms have sat in a gray zone between facilities management, AV and IT," Laleeuwe points out. "They were physical spaces first with technology added into them over time, so they were rarely managed by IT departments with the same level of telemetry as laptops, servers or network infrastructure." The impact of reactive tech support IT professionals could often tell whether a device was connected to the network, but struggled to see how the room was being used or whether it delivered a reliable user experience. That lack of visibility explains why meeting room tech support has often been reactive, with staff only intervening once something breaks. "A room was assumed to be working until someone complained that a call wouldn't start, the audio was poor, a display failed, or remote participants couldn't follow the conversation," Laleeuwe says. "Without reliable data on usage, performance and failure patterns, IT had limited ability to predict issues, prioritize investments or optimize rooms before users were affected." The situation had knock-on effects at various levels. For employees, faulty technology creates immediate friction: meetings start late, participation becomes difficult, and unsecured personal devices get pressed into service as a fallback. An additional challenge in a hybrid world is that meeting room technology acts as a bridge between remote and in-office colleagues, so when it fails, the meeting fails with it. For IT teams, poorly maintained technology produces operational inefficiency. Rather than working to make collaboration environments more effective, they end up firefighting individual incidents. For the business itself, a lack of activity data makes facilities planning considerably harder. "Some spaces may be over-engineered with technology that's barely used, while others are under-equipped for the way people actually collaborate," Laleeuwe points out. "This leads to wasted investment, inconsistent user experiences, and missed opportunities to design rooms around real behavior rather than just assumptions." The value of telemetry Endpoint monitoring technology, such as ClickShare's XMS Cloud Management Platform, changes that picture. Organizations can measure occupancy patterns and how their meeting rooms are used in practice, track equipment uptime, connection quality, and software and firmware status, and follow adoption levels alongside the volume and type of support incidents raised. The data helps IT professionals judge not only whether a room is operating effectively in a technical sense, but whether it is delivering the experience employees expect. As Laleeuwe explains: "Telemetry changes meeting room management from a reactive discipline into a proactive one. Instead of waiting for users to report problems, IT can identify patterns, spot underperforming rooms, detect device issues, plan maintenance and make investment decisions based on evidence." In other words, meeting rooms can be treated as managed endpoints, with IT monitoring, patching, securing, supporting, and assessing them against clear performance indicators. That matters because meeting rooms are now hubs where business-critical work happens, not just spaces where calls take place. "They influence productivity, employee experience, meeting equity, collaboration culture, and return on workplace investments," Laleeuwe adds. "When IT has better visibility and control, employees get more reliable rooms, IT teams reduce support overhead, and the business can make smarter decisions about workplace design, technology standardization, and future upgrades." IT shapes organization-wide collaboration While the benefits of such technology are clear, the approach requires IT teams to develop a broader range of skills than traditional device support. Endpoint management, networking, security, and lifecycle management all remain essential, but that expertise must now be combined with AV knowledge, an understanding of acoustics, data analysis, workplace experience design, and change management. This mix of skills "changes IT's role", Laleeuwe indicates, because teams are no longer just fixing what has broken. "They're helping shape how collaboration happens across the organization," she explains. "That means interpreting room data, understanding user behavior, working more closely with workplace, HR, facilities and sustainability teams, and influencing standards for how meeting spaces are designed and used." These skills are best developed through cross-functional collaboration and closer partnerships with AV specialists and vendors, Laleeuwe advises. Rather than regarding room analytics as isolated device data, she recommends treating them as part of a broader palette of workplace intelligence. That makes it easier to improve business performance by understanding how physical spaces, digital tools, people, and their daily tasks interact. AI takes meeting rooms to a new level The introduction of AI-driven meeting environments is expected to reshape meeting room experiences further still. Laleeuwe explains: "AI is moving beyond novelty features, such as basic transcription, and becoming part of the operational layer of collaboration. In the room, this can include intelligent camera framing, noise reduction, audio calibration, live transcription, translation, automated notes, action item tracking, room diagnostics and performance optimization." The real value of the technology is that it reduces user friction while improving outcomes. Better audio and video input, for instance, makes AI-generated summaries and follow-up actions more accurate. Room-level intelligence helps meetings start more quickly and become more inclusive, while giving IT teams insight into where collaboration is working well and where it is breaking down. Return on technology, Laleeuwe advises, is better measured through outcomes than by counting the number of AI features a particular room can boast. Those outcomes include adoption rates, employee feedback, fewer support requests, improved uptime, time saved, and meeting effectiveness. Another consideration is that AI can support organizations' sustainability and "doing more with less" agendas by turning room and device data into a tool for practical decision-making. IT as a key source of ESG intelligence That is because meeting room analytics reveal which devices consume resources without delivering value, where standardization could reduce duplication, and whether longer lifecycle planning could avoid unnecessary replacements. In other words, sustainability becomes more measurable. "Instead of relying only on high-level ESG [environmental, social and governance] commitments, organizations can look at concrete indicators, such as energy-related behavior, consolidation opportunities, and the environmental impact of technology choices across many rooms," Laleeuwe says. "AI can help surface patterns that would be difficult to see manually, giving IT and workplace teams a stronger basis for decisions that reduce waste, extend product lifecycles, and improve operational efficiency." She believes AI and telemetry will strengthen the strategic position of IT leaders in ESG discussions. As connected devices, collaboration platforms, and workplace systems generate more sustainability data, "IT becomes one of the few functions able to connect operational technology choices to measurable environmental outcomes", Laleeuwe says. That in turn creates a political shift inside the organization. IT is no longer viewed as an implementation function that simply responds to procurement, facilities management, or business requests, but as a key source of ESG intelligence. That intelligence will help executives understand how everyday technology decisions affect energy use, device lifecycles, electronic waste, workplace efficiency, and long-term resilience. It will also push IT leaders to work more closely with sustainability, finance, workplace and procurement colleagues to turn insight into strategic outcomes. As Laleeuwe concludes: "Their influence will grow, but so will the expectation that technology investments are justified not only by performance and cost, but also by measurable contributions to both business and sustainability goals." 189a4290cdf5516f: South Korean president Lee Jae Myung has told the nation’s cabinet that it’s time to develop AI-powered defensive tools to combat AI-wielding attackers. “Recently, a series of personal information leak incidents have been occurring at financial and public institutions,” he said yesterday – likely referring to incidents like the breach at e-tailer Coupang and last week’s raid on local banks that exposed customer data. “Circumstances indicate that artificial intelligence was utilized, causing great concern and anxiety among the public,” he claimed. “I request that the relevant authorities swiftly and clearly identify the circumstances of these incidents, and rapidly deploy and concentrate the necessary personnel and resources to minimize damage,” he added, before calling for South Korea’s government to “build security capabilities that can detect attacks in advance and preemptively block them.” “I urge the relevant ministries to quickly inspect the security systems across the entire national core infrastructure, as well as the private sector, and immediately implement any necessary security measures,” he continued. “I hope we can accelerate the development and distribution of AI technologies specifically tailored for cybersecurity.” President Lee thinks South Korea needs to “completely innovate our society's security paradigm to fit the AI era.” That work will involve public and private sector players collaborating “to transform our technology, systems, and awareness.” The remarks amount to a major policy statement, and a very public one at that. South Korean ministers and tech giants now get to turn the president’s words into action, a complex task given the broad scope of the leader’s demands and the fact that nobody thinks it's possible to defeat cybercrime. Meanwhile, Down Under Also yesterday, Australian politicians had their chance to grill OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon, who fronted a parliamentary committee to answer questions about how his company’s agents accessed a government medical records website. Kwon allowed that OpenAI should have done better than emailing the abuse reporting email address at the relevant Australian government agency but defended the company’s efforts to learn from the Hugging Face incident. The committee is sitting for another two days this week, with one topic of debate being how or if Australia should tweak its copyright laws to ensure AI companies pay content creators whose works they use when training their models. Australian law doesn’t include a fair use provision like those that AI companies in the USA relied on when sourcing content. Creators fear a rumored opt-in payments scheme will be too weak, but Australia’s government fears it may miss out on big datacenter investments and access to onshore frontier models if it doesn’t change copyright law to make it more AI-friendly. ®
c6e2c815c232e7d5: Microsoft has updated the lifecycle of an Azure instance, without offering any information on how long it takes for an instance type to expire. Redmond’s “enhanced lifecycle” landed in late September in a post that explains the four phases in the life of a cloudy VM: Current – VMs are recommended for new deployments, are available in many regions, and receive standard maintenance and support; Extended – Still supported, but may be subject to usage quotas and unspecified “changes to purchasing options and pricing.” Microsoft recommends planning a move to Current VMs. End of Life – VMs are still supported but are only available to existing customers and you may not be able to get more of the instances you want. Once VMs reach this stage, Microsoft wants you “actively” working to shift workloads onto Current or Extended VMs. Retired – Unsupported but not quite dead. Microsoft says VMs in this phase are no longer available and have been “deallocated” – Azure-speak for not having an IP address and being dormant, with data preserved. Customers can’t provision the instance types. Microsoft’s post explains that the company defined this lifecycle because it is “committed to helping you navigate these infrastructure transitions and take advantage of the next wave of innovation.” The post includes many mentions of “modernization” – the process of moving to Current Azure instance types. “As Azure continues to advance, our commitment is to make change predictable, transparent, and supported through clear lifecycle guidance, early visibility, and practical help to modernize with confidence,” the post states. The mention of “predictable” change led The Register to wonder if the lifecycle has a predictable cadence that means users can expect that instance types will remain in “Current” status for a certain number of years. We asked Microsoft if its Azure instance lifecycles are timed, and a spokesperson sent the following comment: “As Azure continues to innovate, we regularly evolve our infrastructure to give customers access to newer technologies and capabilities. As part of our updated Azure Virtual Machines lifecycle, we will continue to provide customers with advance notice when select older-generation VM series enter the End of Life stage. We’re giving customers time, guidance and resources to plan their transition to the current VM generations, while continuing to support Azure VMs through their lifecycle in alignment with the policies we published.” The spokesperson added that Microsoft customers are “notified directly about their specific VM retirements.” For what it’s worth, Microsoft publishes retirement announcements for Azure services. The company has also previously revealed it runs Azure servers for six years. It is unclear if the new Azure lifecycle is tied to that hardware retirement schedule. What is clear is that Microsoft wants Azure customers to regularly consider moving to its latest instance types. That’s a reasonable suggestion given that newer VMs will likely use more powerful processors. There’s also plenty of upside for Microsoft because more recent silicon typically offers more cores per die, and better performance-per-watt. Microsoft therefore gets greater processor density with lower energy consumption, which lowers its operating costs. Let’s see if Redmond’s lifecycle tweaks also see it pass on those savings. ®
4f8b260b4ed41c37: Ahad lalu sebelum bermulanya Grand Prix Bahrain di Sepang, pengulas Sky Sports Martin Brundle bertanya PMX kemungkinan Malaysia menganjurkan semula perlumbaan F1 pada masa depan. Umum tahu kali terakhir perlumbaan itu dianjurkan Malaysia di litar Sepang ialah pada 2017. Nine long years ago.
"Itu harapan saya. Kami sedang berbincang," jawab Anwar Ibrahim. Meskipun jawapan perdana menteri ringkas, ia menggembirakan ramai yang berharap F1 akan kembali ke Sepang.

'Ramai' yang saya maksudkan termasuk pemandu F1 sendiri, tentunya peminat dalam dan luar negara serta pengulas sukan termasuk Brundle yang merupakan bekas pemandu F1. Kesimpulannya mereka merindui Sepang. Dengan GP Bahrain diadakan dengan jayanya dan penuh drama Ahad lalu, their calls are getting louder.

Bagaimanapun seperti yang pernah dikata oleh CEO Sepang International Circuit Azhan Shafriman Hanif, "apabila kita lepaskan Formula 1 ia sangat sukar untuk dapatkan semula". Apa tidaknya. Kalendar tahunan F1 mempunyai had bilangan perlumbaan yang ketat. Apabila Malaysia melepaskan slotnya, banyak negara seluruh dunia masuk queue dan bersaing untuk merebut slot yang ditinggalkan. Oleh itu jika Malaysia serius mahu membawa F1 kembali ke Sepang, negara terpaksa masuk a long waiting list, di samping mengambil kira faktor kos yang amat tinggi dan kos-kos lain yang meningkat. This is stating the obvious, tak perlulah dihuraikan.

Oleh kerana F1 dan Sepang sedang rancak diperkatakan ramai, mari imbau kembali persoalan Malaysia lepaskan F1 in the first place. Kata Najib Razak, waktu itu memegang jawatan perdana menteri, kerajaan beliau terpaksa menamatkan kontrak penganjuran mulai 2018 berikutan pulangan menurun kepada negara berbanding 1999.

"Kerajaan terpaksa tanggung kos penganjuran yang sangat tinggi setiap tahun tetapi pulangan semakin berkurangan termasuk dari segi penonton dan jumlah pelancong asing," kata Najib dipetik media waktu itu. Rasanya ramai masih ingat kata-kata itu. Dalam bahasa mudah: berniaga tak untung.

Tentunya ramai juga yang ingat (kalau lupa sila buat carian Google) Khairy Jamaluddin, ketika itu menteri belia dan sukan, antara individu terawal yang mencadangkan agar Malaysia menghentikan penganjuran F1. Carian Google memaparkan bahawa pada Oktober 2016 Khairy mengeluarkan kenyataan terbuka di Twitter (sekarang X) yang menyarankan kontrak penganjuran di Litar Antarabangsa Sepang ditamatkan. Antara alasan dan hujahnya: Kos terlalu tinggi, pulangan terhad (cited by Najib also), kejatuhan jualan tiket dan penonton televisyen (sedikit sebanyak senada dengan Najib) dan kehilangan kelebihan eksklusif atau novelty.

Sebaliknya Khairy berkata fokus kewangan dan sokongan kepada perlumbaan MotoGP "yang terbukti jauh lebih popular, sentiasa dipenuhi penonton tempatan serta menyaksikan penglibatan pelumba muda Malaysia".

Saya setuju dengan pandangan itu kecuali MotoGP jauh lebih popular daripada F1. Ini tidak tepat. Dua-dua perlumbaan ada peminat tersendiri lantas dua-dua popular. Soal A lebih popular daripada B tidak timbul. Apa pun, alasan kos tinggi yang diberi Najib dan Khairy semasa menamatkan kontrak penganjuran F1 dulu saya akui. Memang kos tinggi dan boleh terus meningkat sekali gus memberi kesan kepada pentadbiran Najib.

Yang saya tidak faham mengapa (menurut Najib dan Khairy) jumlah penonton dan pelancong asing tidak seramai yang diharapkan lantas drop in ticket sales dan penonton televisyen. Pelik kerana setiap perlumbaan F1 di semua litar ia diadakan menyaksikan ia sentiasa mendpat sambutan penonton yang datang ke litar atau menonton perlumbaan di televisyen. Semua negara yang menganjurkan perlumbaan F1 tidak kehilangan pelancong.

Mengapa Malaysia tidak didatangi ramai pelancong lalu penjualan tiket merosot? Apakah kita tidak semeriah negara lain yang menganjurkan perlumbaan F1? Adakah mungkin Malaysia sendiri tidak kuat membuat promosi untuk Sepang?

Aspek novelty yang diketengahkan Khairy agak pelik. Menurut beliau Sepang hilang sinar dengan adanya litar di negara lain seperti Singapura, China, Bahrain dan Abu Dhabi. Khairy mengakui GP Singapura lebih bijak menarik pelancong dengan konsep perlumbaan malam di tengah kota (street race) yang disertakan dengan konsert antarabangsa. Sebaliknya Sepang kekal perlumbaan siang di bawah matahari terik dan kedudukan litar yang jauh dari bandar raya, katanya.
Ya memang Singapura bijak tetapi apa respon kita? Tutup kedai -- hentikan perlumbaan F1 di Sepang. Perlu dinyatakan street races have their share of detractors. Saya tak cadang perincikan.

Mengenai perlumbaan di Sepang diadakan dalam cuaca panas, saya pernah baca laporan yang memetik beberapa pelumba terkemuka menyifatkan Sepang sebagai the hottest circuit in the F1 series. Namun elemen panas dicampur dengan bentuk litar membuatkan Sepang cabaran which they look forward to take on. Di Sepang it's a test for both machine and driver.

Litar Sepang masih di lokasi sama -- jauh daripada Kuala Lumpur. Semasa GP Bahrain diadakan tempoh hari, 100,000 penonton datang. Perlumbaan dianjurkan oleh Bahrain tetapi Malaysia mendapat economic spillover yang menguntungkan. Jadi untuk mengatakan kedudukan Sepang menyumbang kepada kurang penonton dan F1 kurang dapat sambutan di Malaysia boleh dipertikaikan.

Bukan tujuan penulisan ini mengungkit kisah lama cuma saya teringat laporan myMetro 1 Julai lalu mengenai pelanjutan kontrak penganjuran MotoGP di Sepang. Malaysia akan terus menjadi tuan rumah MotoGP dari 2027 hingga 2031 di Litar Antarabangsa Sepang. Semasa membuat pengumuman itu, CEO SIC berkata SIC tidak mahu ulangi kesilapan menamatkan kontrak F1 pada 2018.

Saya tutup penulisan ini dengan memetik perenggan akhir artikel Pengerusi Perbadanan Stadium Malaysia Helmy Haja Mydin yang disiar portal Scoop bertajuk 'The Formula for F1's return to Sepang'. Kata beliau: "Sepang has shown it can still host the world. Whether we pay to do so every year is a question for the spreadsheet and it should be answered there first".

0a32c83147aaa1e5: Only a week after warning about the perils of competitor Z.ai's GLM-5.3 model and its advanced cybersecurity capabilities, Anthropic has expanded its Cyber Verification Program (CVP) – or rather, reconfigured it. "For the past six months, we’ve enabled trusted access through two programs: Project Glasswing and the CVP," the AI biz said. "Now, we’re integrating these programs into one expanded offering, designed to give more security organizations access to the capabilities they need to protect their systems." Project Glasswing and CVP launched in April 2026 alongside the debut of Mythos, the company's highly capable and equally hyped frontier model. Project Glasswing gave partners early access to Mythos so they could scour their systems for vulnerabilities before attackers beat them to it. VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity was not particularly impressed with CVEs identified by Project Glasswing, noting that fewer than 0.5 percent of the 225 Anthropic-linked vulnerabilities he tracked were being exploited in the wild. And Anthropic's own warning last month about the risks posed by GLM-5.3 somewhat undermines the idea that there's anything special about its own Mythos model. Even so, Anthropic says that its security program has allowed its partners to spot at least 129,000 verified software vulnerabilities between April and July 2026. And the biz claims that its own open source scanning efforts revealed an additional 5,500 verified vulnerabilities between April and October. "Of these verified vulnerabilities, more than 33,000 have so far been rated as critical- or high-severity," Anthropic said. "This is likely an undercount, as it is based on survey data from only a subset of Glasswing partners. As such, we expect the true impact to be at least five times higher." When these might get patched is unclear. The company's own figures indicate that of 5,674 true positive vulnerabilities, 3,014 are high severity, and 1,522 are critical severity, yet only 516 have been patched. Given industry boasting about the cybersecurity prowess of AI models, generating a fix, testing it, and deploying it ought to be nearly automatic at this point. But the gap between identification and remediation suggests there's a lot of slack in the system that needs to be ironed out. Two programs into one with three tiers Now Anthropic's two programs, one intended for organizations and one for individual security professionals, have been merged and reconfigured into three tiers. The AI biz has not explained why, but its stated intent is to tie model capabilities to specific tasks: Defense Access, Red Team Access, and Specialized Access. Depending on the tier, participants will encounter more or fewer blocks on security-related tasks. As a measure of program participation value, Anthropic said that based on five attempts at 10 CyScenarioBench challenges, those without CVP access got blocked on every attempt. Defense Access is intended for security teams at companies, nonprofits, universities, and government organizations that focus on system defense. In this tier, Claude Opus 5.5 faced refusals in 46 of 50 attempts and succeeded four times. Red Team Access is for penetration testing and offensive cyber evaluation, and participants will still face model refusals for model interactions that would cause physical harm or mass disruption. Specifically, Claude Opus 5.5 completed 34 of the 50 tasks with Red Team Access safeguards enabled, a rate similar to what would be expected from Specialized Access. Specialized Access sounds like a rebranding of Glasswing – it's "reserved for a limited set of verified organizations that are authorized to test safety systems that could impact people’s lives or disrupt markets, such as flight operating systems, power grids, telecom networks, interbank transfer infrastructure, and government administrative networks." Those granted admission to this exclusive tier will face the fewest model refusals, not counting anyone using abliterated open-weight models that have had their guardrails suppressed. For the next month or two, program participants will need to allow their data to be retained by Anthropic as part of its AI safety requirements. But soonish, the company's Enterprise Frontier Safeguards program will offer zero data retention. Organizations already granted zero data retention while using Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Mythos 5.1 can participate in CVP under those same terms.®
5aab7bda8d58cc55: When the United States and China begin agreeing on the vocabulary of their strategic relationship, Asean should pay close attention.
The September summit between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping produced two developments of particular importance.

Washington and Beijing agreed to establish a dialogue on what the United States now calls “super intelligence” (SI), accompanied by a bilateral communication channel for serious SI incidents. The next SI summit is in November 2026.
Second, the relationship was framed in official Chinese reporting around a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” The phrase is important.
It suggests that the two largest powers are attempting to place intense competition within a framework where cooperation remains possible.
This should not be mistaken for a formal alliance or strategic partnership.

But politically, the language points towards treating China as a constructive strategic interlocutor — and potentially a constructive strategic partner where common interests converge — rather than merely an adversary that must be contained.
Asean should understand the significance.

For years, US-China relations have been defined largely through rivalry: tariffs, semiconductors, Taiwan, the South China Sea, military competition and technological restrictions. None of these disagreements has disappeared.
Yet Washington and Beijing are simultaneously discovering that certain technologies may become too consequential to manage exclusively through competition.
Super intelligence is potentially one of them.
President Trump announced at the United Nations that his administration would use “super intelligence” rather than artificial intelligence.
Following his meeting with Xi, Trump said the Chinese leader appeared receptive to the terminology, while Beijing indicated that it respected Washington’s choice of wording.
Terminology matters.
“Superintelligence” conventionally has a much narrower technical meaning: Intelligence exceeding human capabilities across virtually all cognitive domains.
The Trump administration appears to be using “super intelligence” more broadly as a replacement for AI. These meanings should not be confused.
Nevertheless, the creation of a US-China dialogue on super intelligence is strategically serious.
The two powers are beginning to discuss the risks and benefits associated with advanced AI while creating a channel through which serious incidents can potentially be communicated.
This resembles, conceptually rather than technologically, an embryonic form of crisis management.
During the nuclear age, Washington and Moscow eventually realised that strategic competition required communication precisely because miscalculation could become catastrophic.
AI is not a nuclear weapon. Its development, diffusion and applications are fundamentally different.

Yet the strategic principle is familiar: As technology becomes more powerful, misunderstanding between the powers controlling much of it becomes increasingly dangerous. Asean must therefore be warned.
If Washington and Beijing become the principal architects of the rules surrounding super intelligence, Southeast Asia risks becoming a rule-taker rather than a rule-shaper.
Asean represents almost 700 million people and is rapidly attracting data centres, semiconductor investments, cloud infrastructure and AI-related industries.
Yet much of the frontier technology, computing capacity and foundational architecture remains controlled outside Southeast Asia.
Technological dependence can eventually become strategic dependence.
Asean therefore needs its own position on super intelligence.
This does not mean attempting to compete directly with the United States or China.
Such an ambition would be unrealistic. Malaysia's strength, in particular, has always rested on what can be called Quiescent Diplomacy.
It uses a silent but strategic approach to create sufficient diplomatic and institutional space so that larger powers recognise the importance of Southeast Asia including AI and SI.
Asean, invariably , Malaysia, should insist on meaningful human control over autonomous systems.
This involves stronger cyber security standards. Just as importantly sovereign protection of data. Due safeguards are required to protect critical infrastructure.
As and when regional protocols for dealing with major AI incidents are made more resilient, the region can handle the dawn of the age of SI.
Asean should also use Asean Plus Three, the East Asia Summit and other Asean-led mechanisms to ensure that conversations about advanced AI do not become an exclusively US-China enterprise.
The emerging US-China rapprochement over terminology and strategic stability is encouraging. But it also contains a warning.
Washington and Beijing remain strategic competitors.
Yet they are demonstrating that, where systemic dangers demand it, competition can coexist with constructive strategic cooperation.
Asean must ensure that it has a seat at the table when the rules governing those dangers are written.
The age of artificial intelligence has arrived. If the age of super intelligence follows, Asean cannot afford to wake up after Washington and Beijing have already determined its rules.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
493135852c550b1f: Google on Tuesday struck a deal with Constellation Energy for 3,590 megawatts of future energy supply, including nearly a gigawatt of new nuclear capacity, as the search and advertising giant tries to find enough energy to power its datacenter ambitions. The 20-year power purchase agreement will see Constellation, the largest purveyor of atomic energy in the US, bring an additional 890 megawatts of nuclear capacity online by making "targeted investments at multiple nuclear plants." We understand those investments will go toward upgrades to at least 11 existing nuclear plants across Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey through a process known as uprating. "By modernizing and upgrading turbines, steam generators, and digital control systems at operating plants, uprates deliver substantial capacity gains without the multi-year timelines or interconnection bottlenecks associated with greenfield construction," the power company explained in a statement. The other 2,700 megawatts the deal covers will come from other unspecified sources. Constellation expects to spend $4.3 billion to fulfill its side of the deal, and plans to complete its first uprated reactor by 2028. Google is on track to spend as much as $205 billion on datacenters and compute this year, but all that money is wasted if it can't secure power to make its servers and GPUs work. The hyperscaler is far from the only one scrambling to secure adequate power to keep its AI ambitions from starving. Microsoft also tapped Constellation to reignite the Three Mile Island Unit 1 reactor – you know, the one that didn't partially melt down back in 1979. That reactor is expected to come online as early as next year. Meta is also making noise about nuclear. The Social Network is working with Constellation to save a doomed nuclear plant in Illinois. Earlier this year, Meta revealed that its nuclear and clean energy commitments now total 6.6 gigawatts, though it's worth noting that figure depends heavily on the successful rollout of small modular reactors, an unproven form of miniature nuke plant. ®
1ab22332aa9b2687: Jet-powered Russian drones recently hit a train in Ukraine a mere mile from the Polish border. The drone pilots, and their Kremlin minders, must have known that officials from Europe, the UK, the US, and elsewhere had previously left Kyiv by train after participating in the Yalta European Strategy (YES) Annual Meeting, a sort of Ukrainian Davos.

But the trains carrying former UK prime minister Boris Johnson, former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, former CIA director David Petraeus, and former Polish president Aleksander Kwaśniewski, among others, were not hit. Had the Russians missed them intentionally or through incompetence?
Whatever the answer, there is no doubt that Western officials’ continued support for Ukraine, on display at the YES Annual Meeting, rankles the Kremlin.

At the end of one panel, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski candidly remarked that, if attacked, Nato could defeat Russia quite quickly: “If the Ukrainians have knocked out half of Russia’s refining capacity in six months, we could do it in six weeks and take out the other half.” Sikorski later confirmed that he was referring to Nato’s European members.
The Kremlin was stunned by this matter-of-fact remark and quickly went on the offensive, with Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova calling it “Russophobia”.

Perhaps Kremlin officials have grown accustomed to friendly exchanges with US president Donald Trump’s so-called “negotiators,” Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner—blind amateurs “unburdened with geopolitical detail,” as Edward Luce put it in the Financial Times.
Viktor Sobolev, a member of the State Duma Defense Committee, dismissed the premise: “We don’t plan to attack anyone; the president has said this many times.”

Never mind that Russian president Vladimir Putin also vehemently denied that he had any intention of invading Ukraine and, before that, Georgia. To make his point more clearly about how inoffensive Russia was, Sobolev went on to warn Poles against picking a fight with “a country that possesses nuclear weapons”.

The most pathetic comment came from Putin’s aide Nikolai Patrushev, who accused Sikorski of “Russophobic frenzy” and claimed that Russia poses no threat to anyone because it has no reason to conduct military operations against Europe.

But if Russia were to attack Poland, he added, the country would cease to exist within 2–3 days. (In a subsequent TV interview, Sikorski dismissed Patrushev’s threat, remarking that “2–3 days” is how long it was supposed to take Russia to occupy Kyiv back in 2022.)

The Kremlin is determined to isolate Ukraine. That means not only breaking the will of the country’s backers, but also cutting it off physically by striking merchant ships on the Black Sea and shelling Odesa’s three main ports.

This has paralysed the export of grain at the peak of an exceptional harvest and prevented even the cautious movement of cargo along the coast of Romania and Bulgaria, which will have consequences for Ukraine’s economic survival and world food prices.
Making matters worse, the Danube is so shallow this year that its river ports are practically unusable. And those vessels small enough to enter it risk coming under fire.
A civilian cargo boat en route to Galați, Romania, was recently hit by a Russian drone at the mouth of the Danube, killing the captain and several crew members.

Overland routes are also being disrupted by Russian attacks on Ukrainian border posts. The Starokozache crossing, which leads into Moldova, was recently hit; so was the Mayaki bridge on the same route.
The closures of border checkpoints, no matter how brief, can turn waiting trains and cars into sitting ducks for even the most inexperienced drone operators.

Roads may be slightly less dangerous than rail tracks because itineraries can be changed on short notice. Petraeus, one of the officials almost struck by a Russian drone when leaving Kyiv by train, suggested that next time he might take a car.

These assaults cannot go unanswered, because they isolate Ukraine and embolden Putin to continue testing the West. After this recent train bombing, Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte was asked about the possibility of a Russian attack that could demand the alliance’s response.
He cautioned: “If you are willing to sacrifice 1.2 million of your own people in this crazy unprovoked fight, let’s not be naive about what Putin could do.”

With winter approaching, Ukraine desperately needs help: generators, heaters, warm clothes, and power stations. When the border is shut, bringing aid feels a bit like delivering items for inmates at the prison gates.

But that is precisely what Putin is trying to achieve. He is seeking to destroy an entire country by severing its ties with the outside world. Ukrainians know what awaits them if Putin succeeds. Are the rest of us aware of what we are enabling by failing to act? In Rutte’s words, let’s not be naive.
Anna Husarska, a former senior policy adviser at the International Rescue Committee, is a journalist and political analyst.

70fd9bcc6ab94729: The rivalry between Anthropic and OpenAI, the two leading US AI model makers, is no contest when it comes to assessing which one gives you more value for your subscription money, according to industry research firm SemiAnalysis. Following changes to OpenAI's $200 per month subscription plan that effectively halved its value, SemiAnalysis looked at the various subscription plans offered by AI companies, because that's still the main way that individuals and small businesses buy AI services. AI subscriptions are heavily subsidized – customers get far more tokens for their money than they would paying metered API rates. And SemiAnalysis argues that it's necessary to delve into subscription pricing to evaluate AI shops financially because subscription usage consumes a disproportionate amount of company compute resources. Claude subscriptions, the biz claims, take up about 42 percent of Anthropic's inference compute while generating just 10 percent of its revenue. And those subscriptions provide considerable value. "Anthropic is an overwhelmingly better deal, offering ~5x the API-equivalent value across the board," SemiAnalysis claims in reference to mid-tier models GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. "You could argue that this is unfair for [OpenAI] because 6.1 Sol is much cheaper per token than Opus 5.5, but the gap is still massive even if you switch to comparing the number of tokens." OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment. SemiAnalysis' calculation relies on measuring token output rates, converting those into tokens per 5-hour usage window and per month, and then computing the API-equivalent value. Company researchers contend that API-equivalent value is the best figure for capturing the value of a subscription plan, though they allow that other measures like raw token volume may be more appropriate in some instances. API-based comparisons can be slow to account for the rapidly shifting capabilities of models that come to market. The debut of a new open source model, for example, can alter what's possible at a given price. For those with access to subscription plans, the subsidized prices clearly offer real value, so much so that there's an underground market for reselling tokens from pooled subscription accounts in many parts of the world. But there are other ways to measure AI value. Artificial Analysis, for example, tracks cost per task – the estimated dollar cost of completing a specific task. By that yardstick, GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72) is far more affordable than Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98), at least for those paying API rates. But that ratio may not be true for different tasks – benchmark performance may not reflect your workload. As measured by tokens, Claude Pro ($20 per month) provides 2.9 billion tokens per month, compared to ChatGPT ($20/mo) at 1 billion tokens per month, according to SemiAnalysis. But models may use more or fewer tokens than others for the same task, and when the output is functional, like code, AI output may achieve a similar result across different models but with differing degrees of efficiency. Anticipating AI costs gets more complicated for businesses, which can't count on subscription subsidies and may not have experience with AI cost management. In a July report, McKinsey said 93 percent of enterprises exceeded their AI budgets. "I think all businesses are seeing their AI costs rise," said Dhruv Amin, co-founder of AI agent biz Skydive, in an interview with The Register. Since the beginning of the year, he said, AI has been getting better at solving certain business problems, and companies have started deploying AI more widely, then noticing their token bills going through the roof. "The labs typically subsidize their prosumer plans with subscription pricing massively," said Amin. "And I think it's part of their marketing funnel because more people are able to use the tools, get familiar with the tools, and then bring those tools to work." But for larger companies, he said, two problems arise. You have more employees than can fit on a subsidized plan and, at scale, costs add up fast. "A huge way that enterprises solve this is being able to make a workload work well on the frontier and then quickly switch it to an open source model that they control and that they can serve at a much lower fraction of the cost," he said. "And so for us internally we were able to drop our AI costs 75 percent plus just by moving them all to Skydive Glide, which is our model router that for the given workload tries to find an equivalent open source model that can handle that workload without a quality drop. And so today we run a lot of our workloads on GLM-5.3 Flash." Amin said that companies adept at AI cost management maintain evaluation benchmarks that reflect their workloads. Companies use those metrics to test new models as they come out in whatever AI harness they're using, to ensure consistency. Looking ahead, he said, he expects companies will trust more of that work to service providers. "So what this means is that if you deploy an agent on top of us, we capture in the background the data of how that agent's actually running in production," he said. "And then we use that to construct the eval data set on the fly." ® Updated Oct 6 at 2322 GMT to clarify that Skydive is the platform that sells the agents, while Anything is the umbrella parent company.
21c23ab08aafeb08: As artificial intelligence transforms industries and national security, understanding the latest hardware capabilities is important for maintainind technological advantage. AI accelerators — specialized systems designed to speed up capabilities such as neural networks, deep learning, and machine learning — have been a major area of development for nearly a decade. Since 2018, team from the Lincoln Laboratory Supercomputing Center (LLSC) has been conducting the Lincoln AI Computing Survey (LAICS, pronounced "lace"). Six papers later, LAICS continues to summarize current commercial AI accelerators and compare their peak performance and peak power. "About eight years ago, we saw a sharp rise in the number of research AI accelerators described in research papers and commercial accelerators being announced, and we started to get questions about them from government sponsors of the laboratory's work. That was motivation enough to start the survey," says Albert Reuther, a staff member at the LLSC, which operates and optimizes the high-performance computing systems used by thousands of laboratory research staff. Although AI accelerators are frequently used for processes such as machine learning, they also can enable other parallel applications, such as modeling the functions of molecules and speeding up simulations of fluid dynamics — processes that are very computationally expensive. AI accelerator technology can come in a number of forms: central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), and dataflow accelerators. Each type of accelerator has slightly different capabilities. CPUs can be used for general-purpose computing, while ASICs can perform only very specific tasks. Dataflow accelerators, FPGAs, and GPUs are more flexible and can be configured for a variety of workloads. Efficiency and performance vary across the different types of accelerators depending on how they are designed. The goal of LAICS is to survey the technologies currently on the market and compare them to find the best accelerators for certain needs. Led by Reuther, the LAICS team includes LLSC members Michael Jones, Peter Michaleas, Jeremy Kepner, and Vijay Gadepally. The team also collaborates with researchers across Lincoln Laboratory, including in the Advanced Technology Division and Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance and Tactical Systems Division, to learn how accelerators support research and development for their missions. The first paper in their series studied 57 accelerators, while the latest one looked at more than 120 accelerators. The main metrics the team uses to compare accelerators are the peak performance and power; then they sort accelerators by whether they're on a chip, card, or system. All the data in the papers are drawn from public sources, which can be challenging because some companies prefer to keep their performance and power data private. To keep up to date on the latest in the field, Reuther runs daily news and citation searches that report new technical press articles, company announcements, and industry presentations. "It continues to surprise me how each year another five to 10 startups get funded and announced, and then release new AI accelerators," Reuther says. "One might think that the landscape is saturated enough, but then another batch of innovative accelerators is introduced." In addition to summarizing the performance versus peak power of the current accelerators, each paper explores a new aspect of the field. For example, the paper published in 2022 investigated sources of performance increases, finding that they stem from smaller, denser transistor designs and the use of lower numerical precision (i.e., calculating fewer significant digits). The latest paper examined different architectural choices available, analyzing how the addition of certain components, such as more cores per processor or parallel performance, would change the system. Reuther plans to continue the survey for the foreseeable future, stating that, in just the past few months, six new startups have announced their first AI accelerators. "AI and the hardware it runs on are such hot topics, and it is important for Lincoln Laboratory to be an unbiased technical advisor for choosing and pursuing the right technologies," Reuther says. "Our AI accelerator surveys have helped many sponsors and government colleagues gain a better understanding of the AI accelerator landscape and make better research and acquisition decisions about them. This survey has also been very valuable to determine which GPUs we should consider for upcoming LLSC system purchases so it not only benefits our sponsors and mission programs, but also benefits all LLSC users." The full set of papers and the accompanying datasets can be found here.
ecc07393279513fe: OpenAI will begin automatically watermarking text generated with ChatGPT in the European Union, the company has announced. It will also offer the watermarking feature in other regions, but it will be off by default outside of the EU.

The move in Europe is driven by a need to comply with the EU AI Act, which took effect in August. It requires marking content produced by AI models in a way that another tool can detect. Unfortunately, there is still no completely effective and reliable way to do that. A few standards already exist, like SynthID and the C2PA project, but they are relatively easy to circumvent for anyone with basic know-how.

The same is likely true for OpenAI's watermark. Its method is proprietary; the company calls it textGrain, and has published a technical paper explaining how it works. But in general, it works like other LLM watermarking tools we've seen in the past: It puts patterns in the word choices that are not clear to a human reader and that don't meaningfully change the general quality of the output, but that someone with a key can use a specialized detector to find. OpenAI says it will be giving access to the detector to a limited number of researchers and organizations and providing a request-for-approval process for others to be added over time.
437a29c2809f65ae: President Trump is pushing hard for the US Senate to make daylight saving time permanent so, among other things, golfers can stay on the course longer, but it may not be such a bright idea. New research out of Canada suggests that, even if Americans would get an extra hour of daylight in the evening, the ill health effects of permanent daylight saving time could outweigh the benefits. A paper published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal on Monday reviewed evidence on the health effects of permanent daylight saving time (pDST) as several Canadian jurisdictions move to stop changing their clocks. It finds that the opposite approach - adoption of permanent standard time (pST) - would actually be better for people’s health. Sorry, night owls and after-work social butterflies, but the science simply isn’t with you on this one. “Permanent DST preserves later evening light that may facilitate commuting, recreation, social participation, and some economic activity, but it also prolongs darkness on winter mornings,” the authors note. Prolonged morning darkness doesn't really jibe with the inner workings of the human body and light’s essential role in regulating the circadian rhythm. Sure, no one wants to drive home from work in the dark, but we really need morning light to get us functioning properly. Our circadian rhythms, the authors explain, actually run on a slightly longer schedule than a full day - 24.2 hours. For that reason, we rely on natural sunlight to keep us synchronized with the world around us. Morning light is some of the most important, the authors note, because it jump starts that rhythm, wakes us up and gets us moving. Evening light, on the other hand, delays the circadian rhythm, messing with our sense of “social time” and making it tougher to get to sleep and wake up rested in the morning. The effects of later evening light can show up in sleep, mood, education, and work productivity, the authors noted, and we don’t even need pDST to see some of those associations - we can just look at time zones. Move from east to west in the US or Canada and you’ll get some considerable differences in when the sun rises and sets in a particular time zone - in some cases, sunrise and sunset can differ by more than an hour of clock time across a single time zone. In one study cited by the Canadian analysis, residents on the western side of US time zones, where the sun sets later, got around an hour less sleep a week. The study also estimated that an additional hour of sleep per week was associated with around 5 percent higher long-term earnings. Similar results turned up in a German study, the team noted. Another study found that workers on the western end of US time zones ended up working fewer hours, too. On the educational front, an extra hour of sunlight before school was associated with higher math and reading scores in a Florida study “comparable in magnitude to meaningful class-size reductions.” “Ending biannual clock adjustments may eliminate transition harms that last a few weeks, but the health effects of permanent time are likely to be chronic,” the authors noted. “The preponderance of health evidence favors pST, which would align with the recommendations of sleep and chronobiology societies worldwide.” This isn’t the first time researchers have concluded such. British sleep scientists concluded much the same in 2024, which led to their recommendation to permanently kill DST in favor of a permanent shift to Greenwich Mean Time. That isn’t stopping the US from plowing ahead with plans for pDST, though. The Senate passed a measure to enshrine DST in 2022, but the House never acted on it. This time around, the House has passed its own bill to enact pDST, but the Senate is dithering, leading President Trump to go so far as to post the personal cellphone number of one Republican holdout on social media, Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR), who is opposed to the measure. “No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Cotton explained in a post on X following Trump’s doxxing. He’s right, too: The US has twice enacted pDST - once during World War II, which ended after the war, and again in 1973 as an energy saving measure. Congress curtailed the experiment later in 1974 following public backlash over dark winter mornings. The US isn’t alone in trying and failing at enacting pDST, either, as the Canadian paper points out. Russia adopted pDST in 2011 and reversed it in 2014. Chile tried and reversed it as well. In those cases, the reasons for reversing course varied, but concerns included dark winter mornings, disrupted sleep and body clocks, safety, and public dissatisfaction. It’s unclear whether the US government’s latest attempt at enacting pDST will succeed despite political resistance and scientific evidence that it’s a bad idea, but the researchers sure seem to hope not: They note that, if the US makes such a change, Canada will likely be pressured to conform. At the end of the day, we might all be better off just dealing with a couple of clock changes and some short-term sleep disruption. ®

21ab3d58f3ee6e74: Attackers hijacked three top-level domains and used their control to mint counterfeit TLS certificates for Google and other large organizations, Google said Tuesday.

The attackers launched a series of attacks on the .gh, .sl, and .as country code top-level domains (ccTLDs) and then modified authoritative DNS records for selected domains within those namespaces. By controlling those DNS records, the attackers were able to pass automated domain control validation checks and obtain unauthorized certificates for “several Google domains” and “several leading global brands and widely used online services.” Google said it updated Chrome to block all certificates it identified as unauthorized, and worked with the issuing certification authorities to ensure the unauthorized certificates for Google properties were revoked.
Certificate issuance: The weak link in the chain

TLS certificates are the cryptographic credentials that underpin authentication and encryption protections for websites, mail servers, and other Internet infrastructure. These x.509 certificates use a digital signature to bind a domain name such as google.com to a public key. The public key is publicly available, while the private key is held only by the website operator. When a connection shows that the keys match, the visiting party knows it’s connected to the authentic site rather than an impostor. Possession of unauthorized certificates allows attackers to cryptographically impersonate the affected infrastructure.
6b8f238d52b02bf8: Another week brings yet another open weights model and this one is huge — or at least it is for Europe's AI flag bearer Mistral, which has taken to calling the 1 trillion-parameter large language model (LLM) Le Chonk. Its product name is Mistral Large 4, which is a lot less fun than the cat-meme-inspired "very official" moniker Le Chonk. Nonetheless, the LLM is the French model-dev's biggest open weights release ever. At a trillion parameters, Le Chonk is squarely in frontier territory, and like most modern frontier models, it is multimodal, reasoning, and employs a mixture of experts (MoE) architecture with about 49 billion active parameters to keep serving costs low. Mistral didn't offer any guidance on hardware requirements in its release blog, but the model is still small enough to run reasonably on 8-way GPU boxes like Nvidia's HGX B300 or AMD's MI355X. We know far more about the hardware the model was trained on. According to Mistral, this Chonker was trained using roughly 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs — or around 52 NVL72 racks — in Mistral's own datacenters located in Europe on a corpus spanning more than 160 languages using a combination of supervised pre-training and reinforcement learning. Sovereign AI remains a major focus for Europe and Mistral is clearly cashing in on demand for frontier class models trained and run within Europe's borders. The model itself is currently in preview, but you won't have to wait long for its weights to drop. Mistral expects them to be live on Hugging Face and other model repos within the month. Early testing by independent benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis puts Le Chonk at a major disadvantage relative to OpenAI or Anthropic's flagship models. In the AI guru's intelligence leaderboard, Mistral Large 4 preview sits between DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and OpenAI's entry-level GPT6 Luna models. Having said that, Mistral's latest model outshines the United States' most capable open weights model, Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling, by a significant margin. So when it comes to non-Chinese LLMs you can actually download, Mistral does quite well. As you'd expect, Mistral's own benchmarks tell a far rosier story. Across coding, agentic, finance, and legal benchmarks, the model build shows its latest LLM trading blows with some of the top Chinese offerings from Alibaba, Moonshot, Z.AI, and DeepSeek. You can find their charts here, but as always take them with a grain of salt. One area Mistral is particularly proud of is Le Chonk's performance in cybersecurity workloads. The company claims the model is one of the strongest performers in cybersecurity benchmarks like Artificial Analysis' new Cyber index. This is a dig at proprietary American models from the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, which have a tendency to refuse cybersecurity-related tasks that could be perceived as adversarial. As we previously reported, this is potentially problematic for customers trying to use AI models to red-team their own systems in order to identify vulnerabilities before someone else finds them. "Provider-level refusals can block legitimate vulnerability research and incident response, and where losing access to a capability mid-incident can itself become a critical security risk. ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies," Mistral wrote in a blog post. According to Mistral, Le Chonk is only the first in a series of new models made possible by its €3 billion (about $3.4 billion) Series D funding round last month. The company already expects the model's performance to improve meaningfully as it continues applying reinforcement learning, which suggests a more potent Mistral Large 4.1 could be around the corner. If you'd like to give the model a spin before its weights drop later this month, it's currently available via Mistral's API. ®
